questions.stem: Which statement best describes the default behaviour of Cilium's eBPF NodePort implementation with respect to SNAT?

options.text: It operates in SNAT mode by default, redirecting requests to remote backends on the node's behalf and requiring replies to make an extra hop back for reverse SNAT translation.
It operates in DSR mode by default, with backends replying directly to external clients using the service IP/port as source.
It operates in a hybrid mode by default, using DSR for TCP and SNAT for UDP.
It operates without any address translation by default, relying on the client to route replies.

questions.explanation: By default the eBPF NodePort implementation operates in SNAT mode: the node redirects the request to the remote backend on its behalf by performing SNAT, and replies from the backend make the extra hop back to that node for reverse SNAT translation.

optionRationale.b: DSR mode is not the default; it is enabled by changing loadBalancer.mode to dsr.
optionRationale.c: The hybrid mode is described as an optimisation available with DSR, not as the default.
optionRationale.d: The default explicitly performs SNAT, so it is not translation-free.

citations.title: Direct Server Return (DSR)
citations.quote: By default, Cilium's eBPF NodePort implementation operates in SNAT mode.

questions.stem: A platform team runs Cilium natively, without CNI chaining, and wants to enforce the `kubernetes.io/egress-bandwidth` annotation on individual Pods. At the native host networking devices, which mechanism does Cilium's bandwidth manager use for this egress enforcement?

options.text: EDT (Earliest Departure Time)
An eBPF-based token bucket implementation
TBF (Token Bucket Filter) through the bandwidth CNI plugin
BBR congestion control

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that the `egress-bandwidth` annotation is enforced on egress at the native host networking devices using EDT (Earliest Departure Time). The eBPF-based token bucket implementation is for `ingress-bandwidth`. The bandwidth CNI plugin, which is based on TBF, is not used by Cilium's bandwidth manager, and BBR is a congestion control that the bandwidth manager is a prerequisite for, not the egress enforcement mechanism.

optionRationale.b: This is the mechanism the excerpt associates with ``ingress-bandwidth``, not egress enforcement.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt says Cilium's bandwidth manager does not use the bandwidth CNI plugin, which is based on TBF.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt mentions BBR as congestion control for Pods for which the bandwidth manager is a prerequisite, not as the egress enforcement mechanism.

citations.title: Bandwidth Manager
citations.quote:
The ``egress-bandwidth`` is enforced on egress at
the native host networking devices using EDT (Earliest Departure Time), while the ``ingress-bandwidth``
is enforced using an eBPF-based token bucket implementation.

questions.stem: Which two criteria must a subnet satisfy before it is considered a candidate for a new ENI, before any `subnet-ids` or `subnet-tags` narrowing is applied?

options.text: Its VPC ID matches `spec.eni.vpc-id` and its Availability Zone matches `spec.eni.availability-zone`.
Its VPC ID matches `spec.eni.vpc-id` and it shares a route table with the node's subnet.
Its Availability Zone matches `spec.eni.availability-zone` and it has the most available addresses.
It matches all `subnet-tags` and its Availability Zone matches `spec.eni.availability-zone`.

questions.explanation: The excerpt lists exactly two base criteria for picking a subnet: the VPC ID matching `spec.eni.vpc-id` and the Availability Zone matching `spec.eni.availability-zone`.

optionRationale.b: Route-table matching is a later fallback, not a base candidacy criterion.
optionRationale.c: Having the most available addresses is a tie-break among candidates, not a candidacy criterion.
optionRationale.d: Tag matching is an optional narrowing step, not one of the two base criteria.

citations.title: ENI Creation
citations.quote:
The VPC ID of the subnet matches ``spec.eni.vpc-id``
 * The Availability Zone of the subnet matches
   ``spec.eni.availability-zone``

questions.stem: An engineer configures a LoadBalancer service to use DSR with IPIP dispatch. The service has port 80 and targetPort 8080. What is the expected result?

options.text: The service will not work correctly because IPIP does not carry port information, so the service frontend port must equal the backend target port.
The service will work because IPIP encapsulates the original client packet including the destination port.
The service will work because Cilium uses a Geneve option to transport the service port.
The service will work only if the backend Pods are on nodes labeled service.cilium.io/node=beefy.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that when using IPIP dispatch, the service frontend port must be equal to the backend (target) port because IPIP does not carry port information unlike Geneve. Therefore, port 80 and targetPort 8080 will not work correctly.

optionRationale.b: IPIP encapsulates the packet but does not carry port information, so the original destination port is not preserved for the backend.
optionRationale.c: Geneve uses an option to transport the service IP/port, but IPIP does not; the excerpt explicitly contrasts this.
optionRationale.d: The node label is for selective service node exposure, not for making mismatched ports work with IPIP.

citations.title: Direct Server Return (DSR) with IPIP
citations.quote:
When using the IPIP dispatch, the service frontend port must be equal to the
    backend (target) port given IPIP does not carry port information unlike Geneve.

questions.stem: A cluster administrator needs to completely reset Cilium state, including endpoint state and CNI configuration files, because of a serious issue. They set `clean-cilium-state` to `true` and restart Cilium. What happens to existing endpoints that were managed by Cilium?

options.text: They continue to operate as before, but Cilium will no longer manage them and they may stop working without warning; they must be deleted and reconnected to allow the new Cilium instance to manage them.
They are automatically deleted and recreated by Cilium with new IP addresses.
They are restored with the same IP addresses and continue to be managed by Cilium without interruption.
They are migrated to a new Cilium instance and remain fully managed.

questions.explanation: The `clean-cilium-state` option removes all Cilium state, including unrecoverable information such as all endpoint state, as well as recoverable state such as eBPF state pinned to the filesystem, CNI configuration files, library code, links, routes, and other information. This operation is irreversible. Existing endpoints currently managed by Cilium may continue to operate as before, but Cilium will no longer manage them and they may stop working without warning. After using this operation, endpoints must be deleted and reconnected to allow the new instance of Cilium to manage them.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt does not state that endpoints are automatically deleted and recreated; it says they must be deleted and reconnected manually.
optionRationale.c: This describes `clean-cilium-bpf-state`, not `clean-cilium-state`; the latter removes all state and is irreversible.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt states that Cilium will no longer manage the endpoints, not that they are migrated and remain managed.

citations.title: ConfigMap Options
citations.quote: Removes **all** Cilium state, including unrecoverable information such as all endpoint state, as well as recoverable state such as eBPF state pinned to the filesystem, CNI configuration files, library code, links, routes, and other information. **This operation is irreversible**. Existing endpoints currently managed by Cilium may continue to operate as before, but Cilium will no longer manage them and they may stop working without warning.

questions.stem: An engineer edits the Cilium ConfigMap to change `enable-ipv6` and also updates the `cilium-etcd-secrets` Secret. What must be done for the existing Cilium pods to pick up the latest configuration?

options.text: Restart any existing Cilium pods.
Delete and reconnect all endpoints so that Cilium can manage them again.
Set `clean-cilium-bpf-state` to true and leave it enabled permanently.
Nothing; Cilium watches the ConfigMap and Secret and reloads them automatically.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that any changes performed in the Cilium ConfigMap and in the `cilium-etcd-secrets` Secret will require restarting any existing Cilium pods in order for them to pick up the latest configuration.

optionRationale.b: Deleting and reconnecting endpoints is required after using `clean-cilium-state`, not after an ordinary ConfigMap change.
optionRationale.c: `clean-cilium-bpf-state` is for mitigating serious eBPF map issues and should be turned off again after restarting the daemon; it is not the mechanism for applying configuration.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt explicitly requires a restart of existing Cilium pods; automatic reload is not described.

citations.title: ConfigMap Options
citations.quote:
Any changes that you perform in the Cilium ConfigMap and in
``cilium-etcd-secrets`` ``Secret`` will require you to restart any existing
Cilium pods in order for them to pick the latest configuration.

questions.stem: An engineer runs Cilium's eBPF kube-proxy replacement with socket-LB enabled. A pod has an established connected UDP socket to a Service backend, and that backend is then deleted. What does the Cilium agent do?

options.text: It forcefully terminates the application socket connected to the deleted backend so the application can be load-balanced to active backends.
It leaves the socket untouched and silently drops all further packets from that socket until the application closes it.
It rewrites the socket's destination to the Service cluster IP and keeps the connection alive indefinitely.
It disables socket-LB for that pod and falls back to iptables masquerading for the remainder of the connection.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that when socket-LB is enabled, pods can keep sending traffic to a deleted backend, and Cilium handles this by forcefully terminating application sockets connected to deleted backends so applications can be load-balanced to active backends.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says Cilium forcefully terminates such sockets, not that it leaves them and drops packets.
optionRationale.c: No such rewriting of the destination to the cluster IP is described; the described action is termination of the socket.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt does not describe disabling socket-LB or falling back to iptables in this situation.

citations.title: Limitations
citations.quote:
Cilium agent
      handles such scenarios by forcefully terminating application sockets that are connected
      to deleted backends, so that the applications can be load-balanced to active backends.

questions.stem: An engineer wants to inspect the state and status of the Cilium agent on the node they are logged into, and to validate the state of the eBPF maps directly. Which tool is intended for this?

options.text: The `cilium` command line tool, installed remote from the cluster and using `kubeconfig`.
The Cilium Operator, which manages cluster-wide duties.
The debug CLI client (`cilium-dbg`), which interacts with the REST API of the agent on the same node.
The CNI plugin (`cilium-cni`), which is invoked when a pod is scheduled or terminated.

questions.explanation: The debug CLI client is installed along with the Cilium agent, interacts with the REST API of the agent running on the same node, allows inspecting the local agent's state and status, and provides tooling to access the eBPF maps directly.

optionRationale.a: The ``cilium`` tool is a separate CLI for quick-installing, managing and troubleshooting Cilium on Kubernetes clusters, typically installed remote from the cluster.
optionRationale.b: The operator manages cluster-wide duties and is not a local inspection tool.
optionRationale.d: The CNI plugin is invoked by Kubernetes on pod scheduling or termination; it is not the inspection tool.

citations.title: Cilium
citations.quote:
The debug CLI allows inspecting the
  state and status of the local agent. It also provides tooling to directly
  access the eBPF maps to validate their state.

questions.stem: A CiliumLocalRedirectPolicy has a serviceMatcher for a clusterIP service and does not specify toPorts under redirectFrontend. Which traffic is redirected?

options.text: Traffic for all the service ports.
No traffic, because at least one port must be listed.
Only traffic on port 80.
Only traffic whose port name matches a backend port name.

questions.explanation: When toPorts under redirectFrontend are not specified, traffic for all the service ports is redirected.

optionRationale.b: Omitting toPorts is permitted and widens redirection rather than disabling it.
optionRationale.c: No default port of 80 is stated; the absence of toPorts covers all service ports.
optionRationale.d: Port-name mapping applies when ports are specified, not when toPorts is omitted.

citations.title: ServiceMatcher
citations.quote:
When ``toPorts`` under ``redirectFrontend`` are not specified, traffic for
all the service ports will be redirected.

questions.stem: A platform team runs Cilium in overlay mode and wants to use DSR with IPIP for LoadBalancer services. What is the outcome?

options.text: DSR with IPIP will not work because it requires Cilium to be deployed in arch_direct_routing.
DSR with IPIP works in overlay mode as long as the service frontend port equals the backend port.
DSR with IPIP works in overlay mode only if bpf.lbModeAnnotation is set to true.
DSR with IPIP works in overlay mode but requires the service.cilium.io/node annotation to be set.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that DSR with IPIP requires Cilium to be deployed in arch_direct_routing and will not work in arch_overlay mode. Therefore, in overlay mode it will not work.

optionRationale.b: Matching frontend and backend ports is a prerequisite for IPIP, but it does not override the requirement for arch_direct_routing.
optionRationale.c: bpf.lbModeAnnotation enables annotation-based DSR/SNAT mode selection, but it does not make IPIP work in overlay mode.
optionRationale.d: The service.cilium.io/node annotation is for selective service node exposure, not for enabling IPIP in overlay mode.

citations.title: Direct Server Return (DSR) with IPIP
citations.quote:
It requires Cilium to be deployed in arch_direct_routing, it will not
work in arch_overlay mode.

questions.stem: An engineer sets `clean-cilium-bpf-state` to `true` in the Cilium ConfigMap and restarts the Cilium daemon. What is the effect on existing endpoints and connections?

options.text: All eBPF state is removed from the filesystem on startup; endpoints are restored with the same IP addresses, but ongoing connections may be briefly disrupted and loadbalancing decisions are lost, so active connections via the loadbalancer will break.
All Cilium state, including endpoint state and CNI configuration files, is permanently removed, and existing endpoints must be deleted and reconnected.
eBPF state is preserved, but endpoints are assigned new IP addresses and all connections are re-established automatically.
Only the eBPF state related to loadbalancing is removed; endpoints and ongoing connections are unaffected.

questions.explanation: The `clean-cilium-bpf-state` option removes all eBPF state from the filesystem on startup. Endpoints are restored with the same IP addresses, but ongoing connections may be briefly disrupted and loadbalancing decisions will be lost, so active connections via the loadbalancer will break. The eBPF state is reconstructed from original sources, and the option should be turned off again after restarting the daemon.

optionRationale.b: This describes `clean-cilium-state`, which removes all Cilium state including unrecoverable endpoint state and CNI configuration files, and is irreversible.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt states that endpoints are restored with the same IP addresses, not new ones, and that connections may be disrupted.
optionRationale.d: The option removes all eBPF state, not just loadbalancing state, and it does affect ongoing connections.

citations.title: ConfigMap Options
citations.quote: Removes all eBPF state from the filesystem on startup. Endpoints will be restored with the same IP addresses, but ongoing connections may be briefly disrupted and loadbalancing decisions will be lost, so active connections via the loadbalancer will break.

questions.stem: Neither `spec.eni.security-groups` nor `spec.eni.security-group-tags` is set on the CiliumNode. What Security Groups does the newly created ENI receive?

options.text: It inherits the security group IDs of `eth0` of the instance.
It is created with the account's default Security Group.
It is created with no Security Groups attached.
It inherits the security group IDs of the primary ENI of another node in the same subnet.

questions.explanation: The third step of the computation states that when none of the fields are set, the ENI inherits the security group IDs of `eth0` of the instance.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt names `eth0` inheritance, not the account default Security Group.
optionRationale.c: An ENI with no Security Groups is not described; inheritance from `eth0` is the stated outcome.
optionRationale.d: Inheritance is from `eth0` of the same instance, not from another node.

citations.title: ENI Creation
citations.quote:
Finally if none of the above fields are set then the newly created ENI will
    inherit the security group IDs of ``eth0`` of the instance.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes Kubernetes CRDs in Cilium?

options.text: Due to not depending on any underlying networking limitations, the available addressing space is potentially much larger and allows to run any number of pods per node if the PodCIDR size is configured accordingly.

When running together with an orchestration system such as Kubernetes, the list of all nodes in the cluster including their associated allocation prefix node is made available to each agent automatically. New nodes joining the cluster will automatically be incorporated into the mesh.
All traffic not staying with the ``ipv4-native-routing-cidr`` will be masqueraded to the node's IP address to become publicly routable.

The default choice to store any data and propagate state is to use Kubernetes custom resource definitions (CRDs). CRDs are offered by Kubernetes for cluster components to represent configurations and state via Kubernetes resources.

questions.explanation: The default choice to store any data and propagate state is to use Kubernetes custom resource definitions (CRDs). CRDs are offered by Kubernetes for cluster components to represent configurations and state via Kubernetes resources.

optionRationale.a: This describes Addressing space, not Kubernetes CRDs.
optionRationale.b: This describes Auto-configuration, not Kubernetes CRDs.
optionRationale.c: This describes Masquerading, not Kubernetes CRDs.

citations.title: Data Store
citations.quote: The default choice to store any data and propagate state is to use Kubernetes custom resource definitions (CRDs). CRDs are offered by Kubernetes for cluster components to represent configurations and state via Kubernetes resources.

questions.stem: An engineer creates a LoadBalancer service with the annotation service.cilium.io/forwarding-mode: dsr and sets port: 8080 and targetPort: 80. The service is using DSR with IPIP. What is the likely outcome?

options.text: The service will work because IPIP encapsulates the original packet including the port information.
The service will work because the annotation service.cilium.io/forwarding-mode: dsr overrides the port mismatch.
The service will fail because with IPIP the service frontend port must equal the backend target port.
The service will work but only if the backend pods are on nodes labeled service.cilium.io/node=beefy.

questions.explanation: When using the IPIP dispatch, the service frontend port must be equal to the backend (target) port because IPIP does not carry port information. Therefore port 8080 and targetPort 80 will not work. The other options are incorrect: IPIP does not carry port information, the annotation does not override the port requirement, and node labeling is a separate concern for selective exposure.

optionRationale.a: IPIP does not carry port information; the inner packet retains the original destination port, so the backend must listen on the same port.
optionRationale.b: The annotation selects DSR mode but does not change the port matching requirement.
optionRationale.d: Node labeling is relevant for selective service exposure, not for resolving a port mismatch.

citations.title: Direct Server Return (DSR) with IPIP
citations.quote:
When using the IPIP dispatch, the service frontend port must be equal to the
    backend (target) port given IPIP does not carry port information unlike Geneve.

questions.stem: An engineer wants to use a pool name other than `default` for the migration from cluster-pool to multi-pool IPAM. According to the provided procedure, how should this be configured?

options.text: By setting the `ipam.operator.autoCreateCiliumPodIPPools.<pool-name>` parameters in the Helm upgrade command.
By using the flag `--set-string extraConfig.ipam-default-ip-pool=<pool-name>` in the same Helm upgrade that restarts the operator.
By manually creating a `CiliumPodIPPool` resource with the desired name before running the Helm upgrade.
By modifying the `spec.ipam.podCIDRs` field in the `CiliumNode` resources to reference the new pool name.

questions.explanation: The excerpt explicitly states: 'If you want to use a different default pool name for the migration, configure it globally in the same Helm upgrade that restarts the operator, with `--set-string extraConfig.ipam-default-ip-pool=<pool-name>`.'

optionRationale.a: The `ipam.operator.autoCreateCiliumPodIPPools` parameter is used to define the CIDR and mask size for the pool, but the specific flag for changing the *name* of the default pool is `extraConfig.ipam-default-ip-pool`.
optionRationale.c: The procedure relies on the operator to create the pool automatically (`autoCreateCiliumPodIPPools`), not on manual creation beforehand.
optionRationale.d: The `CiliumNode` resources are updated *after* the migration by the operator; they are not used to configure the migration target pool name.

citations.title: Practical Example
citations.quote: If you want to use a different default pool name for the migration, configure it globally in the same Helm upgrade that restarts the operator, with ``--set-string extraConfig.ipam-default-ip-pool=<pool-name>``.

questions.stem: A cluster has multiple network interfaces on each worker node. An engineer is joining worker nodes to a control-plane node that was initialised with kubeadm init --skip-phases=addon/kube-proxy. What must be ensured for Cilium's kube-proxy replacement to work correctly?

options.text: kubelet's --node-ip is set correctly on each worker
kube-proxy is installed on each worker
The --cri-socket flag is set on each worker
The API_SERVER_IP and API_SERVER_PORT are set on each worker

questions.explanation: The excerpt warns: 'Please ensure that kubelet's --node-ip is set correctly on each worker if you have multiple interfaces. Cilium's kube-proxy replacement may not work correctly otherwise.' Thus, setting --node-ip correctly is necessary.

optionRationale.b: kube-proxy is intentionally skipped; installing it would contradict the goal.
optionRationale.c: The --cri-socket flag is mentioned for kubeadm init, not for worker nodes in this context.
optionRationale.d: API_SERVER_IP and API_SERVER_PORT are used in the Cilium Helm configuration, not on each worker.

citations.title: Quick-Start
citations.quote:
Please ensure that
 `kubelet <https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/command-line-tools-reference/kubelet/>`_'s
 ``--node-ip`` is set correctly on each worker if you have multiple interfaces.
 Cilium's kube-proxy replacement may not work correctly otherwise.

questions.stem: How does the operator determine the interface index for a newly created ENI?

options.text: It scans all existing ENIs and selects the first unused index greater than `spec.eni.first-interface-index`.
It scans all existing ENIs and selects the first unused index greater than or equal to `spec.eni.first-interface-index`.
It uses the number of ENIs currently attached to the instance as the index.
It uses the index of the primary ENI of the instance incremented by one.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that all existing ENIs are scanned and the first unused index greater than `spec.eni.first-interface-index` is selected.

optionRationale.b: The comparison is strictly greater than, not greater than or equal to.
optionRationale.c: Counting attached ENIs is not the described method; the scan looks for the first unused index.
optionRationale.d: The primary ENI's index is not used as the basis for the calculation.

citations.title: ENI Creation
citations.quote:
all existing ENIs are scanned and the first unused index greater than
``spec.eni.first-interface-index`` is selected.

questions.stem: A cluster's kube-apiserver has been configured to use the NodePort range 10000-32767 instead of the Kubernetes default. What must be done on the Cilium side?

options.text: Pass the same range to Cilium via nodePort.range, for example nodePort.range="10000\,32767".
Nothing; Cilium always assumes the default range of 30000-32767.
Set nodePort.autoProtectPortRanges to false so the new range is accepted.
Set nodePort.bindProtection to false so the new range is accepted.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that if kube-apiserver was configured to use a non-default NodePort port range, then the same range must be passed to Cilium via the nodePort.range option, giving nodePort.range="10000\,32767" for a range of 10000-32767.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt gives 30000-32767 only as the default Kubernetes NodePort range; it explicitly requires passing a non-default range to Cilium.
optionRationale.c: autoProtectPortRanges controls whether the NodePort range is appended to the reserved ports, not whether a non-default range is communicated to Cilium.
optionRationale.d: bindProtection controls whether application bind(2) requests to NodePort service ports are prevented, not the port range configuration.

citations.title: NodePort Devices, Port and Bind settings
citations.quote:
If ``kube-apiserver`` was configured to use a non-default NodePort port range,
then the same range must be passed to Cilium via the ``nodePort.range``
option, for example, as ``nodePort.range="10000\,32767"`` for a
range of ``10000-32767``.

questions.stem: A new ENI is being created for an instance whose existing ENIs occupy interface indexes 1, 2 and 4, and `spec.eni.first-interface-index` is set to 1. Which interface index is chosen?

options.text: 1, because it is the value of `spec.eni.first-interface-index`.
3, because it is the first unused index greater than `spec.eni.first-interface-index`.
5, because it is the next index after the highest one in use.
2, because it is the lowest index currently in use and will be reused.

questions.explanation: The excerpt says all existing ENIs are scanned and the first unused index greater than `spec.eni.first-interface-index` is selected. With 1, 2 and 4 in use and a starting point of 1, the first unused index greater than 1 is 3.

optionRationale.a: Index 1 is already in use, and the rule requires an unused index greater than the configured value.
optionRationale.c: The rule takes the first unused index above the configured value, not the one after the highest index in use.
optionRationale.d: Indexes in use are not reused; the scan looks for an unused one.

citations.title: ENI Creation
citations.quote:
all existing ENIs are scanned and the first unused index greater than
``spec.eni.first-interface-index`` is selected.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes Key-Value Store in Cilium?

options.text: When running together with an orchestration system such as Kubernetes, the list of all nodes in the cluster including their associated allocation prefix node is made available to each agent automatically. New nodes joining the cluster will automatically be incorporated into the mesh.

The CNI plugin (``cilium-cni``) is invoked by Kubernetes when a pod is scheduled or terminated on a node. It interacts with the Cilium API of the node to trigger the necessary datapath configuration to provide networking, load-balancing and network policies for the pod.

Encapsulation protocols allow for the carrying of metadata along with the network packet. Cilium makes use of this ability to transfer metadata such as the source security identity. The identity transfer is an optimization designed to avoid one identity lookup on the remote node.

All requirements for state storage and propagation can be met with Kubernetes CRDs as configured in the default configuration of Cilium. A key-value store can optionally be used as an optimization to improve the scalability of a cluster as change notifications and storage requirements are more efficient with direct key-value store usage.

questions.explanation: All requirements for state storage and propagation can be met with Kubernetes CRDs as configured in the default configuration of Cilium. A key-value store can optionally be used as an optimization to improve the scalability of a cluster as change notifications and storage requirements are more efficient with direct key-value store usage.

optionRationale.a: This describes Auto-configuration, not Key-Value Store.
optionRationale.c: This describes Identity context, not Key-Value Store.
optionRationale.b: This describes CNI Plugin, not Key-Value Store.

citations.title: Data Store
citations.quote: All requirements for state storage and propagation can be met with Kubernetes CRDs as configured in the default configuration of Cilium. A key-value store can optionally be used as an optimization to improve the scalability of a cluster as change notifications and storage requirements are more effic

questions.stem: An engineer sets `monitor-aggregation` to `medium` and wants to ensure that, on average, one tracing event is sent during a specific interval, assuming new packets are sent at least once per interval. Which option controls this interval?

options.text: `monitor-aggregation-interval`
`monitor-aggregation`
`debug`
`preallocate-bpf-maps`

questions.explanation: The `monitor-aggregation-interval` option defines the interval to report tracing events. It is only applicable for `monitor-aggregation` levels `medium` or higher. Assuming new packets are sent at least once per interval, this ensures that on average one event is sent during the interval.

optionRationale.b: `monitor-aggregation` sets the aggregation level (none, low, medium, maximum), not the reporting interval.
optionRationale.c: `debug` enables verbose logging and visibility events; it does not control the tracing event interval.
optionRationale.d: `preallocate-bpf-maps` controls pre-allocation of map entries to reduce latency; it does not control the tracing event interval.

citations.title: ConfigMap Options
citations.quote: ``monitor-aggregation-interval`` - Defines the interval to report tracing events. Only applicable for ``monitor-aggregation`` levels ``medium`` or higher. Assuming new packets are sent at least once per interval, this ensures that on average one event is sent during the interval.

questions.stem: An engineer enables Cilium's bandwidth manager on a cluster but leaves legacy routing through the upper stack in place, without BPF Host Routing. What does the guidance warn may result?

options.text: Potentially undesired high latency, so Bandwidth Manager is strongly recommended to be used in combination with BPF Host Routing.
The bandwidth annotations are silently ignored and no rate limiting is applied to any Pod.
Cilium falls back to the bandwidth CNI plugin based on TBF automatically.
Ingress bandwidth enforcement stops working while egress enforcement continues normally.

questions.explanation: The guidance strongly recommends using Bandwidth Manager together with BPF Host Routing, because legacy routing through the upper stack could potentially result in undesired high latency.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt warns of high latency, not of the annotations being ignored.
optionRationale.c: The bandwidth manager does not make use of the bandwidth CNI plugin at all, so no such fallback is described.
optionRationale.d: The warning concerns latency from legacy routing, not a split between ingress and egress enforcement.

citations.title: Bandwidth Manager
citations.quote:
It is strongly recommended to use Bandwidth Manager in combination with
   BPF Host Routing as otherwise legacy routing
   through the upper stack could potentially result in undesired high latency

questions.stem: A platform team exposes an application through a Service of type LoadBalancer with spec.loadBalancerSourceRanges set to 192.168.1.0/24. A pod running in the same cluster connects to the service's external address. What does Cilium's eBPF kube-proxy replacement do with the source-range check for this in-cluster connection?

options.text: It ignores spec.loadBalancerSourceRanges, so the pod is allowed to access the service.
It drops the connection because the pod's IP is not in 192.168.1.0/24.
It allows the connection only if the pod's IP falls within 192.168.1.0/24.
It applies the check only when service.cilium.io/src-ranges-policy is set to deny.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that when a service is accessed from inside a cluster, the kube-proxy replacement ignores spec.loadBalancerSourceRanges regardless of whether the field is set. Consequently, any pod or host process in the cluster can access the LoadBalancer service internally, so the pod is allowed even though its IP is outside the white-listed CIDR.

optionRationale.b: This treats the source-range restriction as applying to in-cluster traffic, but the excerpt says the field is ignored for access from inside the cluster.

citations.quote: When accessing the service from inside a cluster, the kube-proxy replacement will ignore the field regardless whether it is set.

Because the Kubernetes API server rejects any changes to the CIDR maskSize of an active pool.

questions.stem: An engineer defines a LoadBalancer service that uses DSR with IPIP dispatch. The service has port 8080 and targetPort 80. What is the consequence?

optionRationale.b: DNAT occurs on the backend node, but the port mismatch is a prerequisite violation for IPIP dispatch.

questions.stem: An engineer sets `clean-cilium-state` to true and restarts Cilium. Which statement describes the effect on existing endpoints?

questions.stem: An engineer wants to reduce per-packet latency by pre-allocating map entries, accepting the trade-off of up-front memory allocation. Which ConfigMap option should they set to `true`?

options.text: `preallocate-bpf-maps`
`debug`
`monitor-aggregation`
`clean-cilium-bpf-state`

questions.explanation: The `preallocate-bpf-maps` option enables pre-allocation of map entries, which reduces per-packet latency at the expense of up-front memory allocation. It should be set to `true` to optimize for latency. Note that if this value is modified, connectivity may be temporarily disrupted for endpoints with active connections during the next Cilium startup.

optionRationale.b: `debug` enables verbose logging and configures eBPF programs to emit more visibility events; it does not pre-allocate map entries.
optionRationale.c: `monitor-aggregation` controls coalescing of tracing events in `cilium-dbg monitor`; it does not affect map pre-allocation.
optionRationale.d: `clean-cilium-bpf-state` removes eBPF state from the filesystem on startup; it does not pre-allocate map entries.

citations.title: ConfigMap Options
citations.quote: Pre-allocation of map entries allows per-packet latency to be reduced, at the expense of up-front memory allocation for the entries in the maps. Set to ``true`` to optimize for latency.

questions.stem: How does DSR with IPIP transport the service IP and port to the backend, compared with DSR mode with Geneve?

optionRationale.a: That is how Geneve dispatch works, not IPIP dispatch.
optionRationale.b: That describes the IPv4 option / IPv6 extension header dispatch, which IPIP avoids.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says the original client packet with the destination still set to the service IP/port becomes the inner payload.

questions.stem: A cluster is experiencing serious problems with its eBPF maps. An engineer sets `clean-cilium-bpf-state` to true and restarts the Cilium daemon. What is the outcome?

options.text: All eBPF state is removed from the filesystem on startup; endpoints are restored with the same IP addresses, but loadbalancing decisions are lost and active connections via the loadbalancer will break.
All Cilium state is removed, including all endpoint state and CNI configuration files, irreversibly.
eBPF state is preserved and only the endpoint IP addresses are reassigned from the kvstore.
eBPF state is removed, but loadbalancing decisions are retained so that active connections through the loadbalancer continue uninterrupted.

Endpoints are restored with the same IP addresses, but ongoing connections may be briefly disrupted and loadbalancing decisions will be lost, so active connections via the loadbalancer will break. The state is reconstructed from original sources such as Kubernetes or the kvstore.

optionRationale.b: That describes `clean-cilium-state`, which removes all Cilium state including endpoint state and CNI configuration files, and is irreversible.
optionRationale.c: The option removes eBPF state rather than preserving it; reconstruction happens from original sources, not by reassigning addresses.
optionRationale.d: Loadbalancing decisions are lost, not retained, so connections via the loadbalancer break.

questions.stem: A Pod carries the annotations kubernetes.io/egress-bandwidth: "10M" and kubernetes.io/ingress-bandwidth: "20M". How does Cilium's bandwidth manager enforce each of these two limits?

Both egress and ingress are enforced using EDT at the native host networking devices.

optionRationale.b: Only egress uses EDT; ingress uses an eBPF-based token bucket.
optionRationale.c: The mechanisms are the other way round: egress uses EDT and ingress uses the token bucket.
optionRationale.d: The bandwidth manager does not make use of the bandwidth CNI plugin, and TBF is the plugin's mechanism, not Cilium's.

questions.stem: An operator sets `spec.eni.security-groups` and also `spec.eni.security-group-tags` on the CiliumNode. Which security groups end up attached to the newly created ENI?

questions.stem: An operator needs to know which host devices Cilium will treat as native devices for bandwidth enforcement, and wants to override the selection manually. Which description matches the documented behaviour?

questions.stem: An operator wants the operator to attach Security Groups to new ENIs by matching tags rather than by listing IDs. Which field should be set, and what does the operator do with it?

questions.stem: A CiliumNode has neither `spec.eni.subnet-ids` nor `spec.eni.subnet-tags` set, and the node's own subnet has enough free IPs. Where does the operator attempt to create the ENI?

questions.stem: A platform team runs Cilium's eBPF NodePort implementation with the default settings. A client outside the cluster connects to a NodePort service whose backend pod runs on a different node. What does the node receiving the traffic do with the request?

options.text: It redirects the request to the remote backend on its behalf by performing SNAT, and replies from the backend make an extra hop back to that node for reverse translation.
It leaves the packet untouched and the backend replies directly to the external client using the service IP/port as source.
It drops the request because the backend is remote and no tunnel protocol is configured.
It rewrites the destination to the service's externalIP and requires the MTU to be lowered before forwarding.

It immediately re-addresses every running pod from `10.20.0.0/16` without any further action being taken.

The update is accepted rather than rejected, and running pods are not re-addressed automatically: the restriction exists precisely to prevent pods from receiving IPs from a new range while some pods still use the old IP pool on the same nodes. questions.stem: A platform team runs Cilium on nodes whose devices are auto-detected, and Cilium selects more than a single device to expose NodePort. questions.stem: A cluster uses DSR with IPIP together with selective service node exposure. The LoadBalancer service is exposed only on nodes labelled service.cilium.io/node=beefy. Where must the backend Pods run?

options.text: On any node in the cluster, because the load balancing node fully translates the traffic.
On nodes that are part of the exposure set, because the backend node terminates the inbound IPIP traffic and rewrites the reply.
Only on nodes that host neither the LoadBalancer frontend nor any backend.
On nodes without the service.cilium.io/node=beefy label, to avoid conflicts.

questions.explanation: With DSR the backend node is part of the service handling: it terminates the inbound IPIP traffic and rewrites the reply so that it is sourced from the service address. This requires the service to be present on the backend node, so when DSR IPIP is combined with selective service node exposure, the backend Pods must run on nodes that are part of the exposure set.

optionRationale.a: That describes SNAT forwarding, where the load balancing node fully translates the traffic and the backend node takes no part in service handling.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt says only nodes that host neither the LoadBalancer frontend nor any backend may be left out of the exposure set; it does not say backends must run there.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says backend Pods must run on nodes that are part of the exposure set, here nodes labelled service.cilium.io/node=beefy.

questions.stem: An existing cluster is running kube-proxy as a DaemonSet. An engineer wants to remove kube-proxy to prepare for Cilium's eBPF kube-proxy replacement. Which sequence of commands should they use?

options.text: kubectl -n kube-system delete ds kube-proxy; kubectl -n kube-system delete cm kube-proxy; iptables-save | grep -v KUBE | iptables-restore
kubectl -n kube-system delete ds kube-proxy; kubectl -n kube-system delete cm kube-proxy; iptables-save | grep KUBE | iptables-restore
kubectl -n kube-system delete ds kube-proxy; kubectl -n kube-system delete cm kube-proxy; iptables -F
kubectl -n kube-system delete ds kube-proxy; kubectl -n kube-system delete cm kube-proxy; systemctl restart kubelet

questions.explanation: The excerpt provides the exact commands: delete the kube-proxy DaemonSet, delete the kube-proxy ConfigMap to avoid reinstallation during a kubeadm upgrade, and run on each node with root permissions: iptables-save | grep -v KUBE | iptables-restore. This removes KUBE-related iptables rules.

$ # Run on each node with root permissions:

questions.stem: A KataPod is created inside the VM that Kata runs in the outer Container Networking Namespace. What does Kata copy into the inner Container Networking Namespace's eth0?

Only the default route MTU, while the outer eth0 device MTU is ignored.
Neither value; the inner namespace inherits the MTU of the underlying network.

optionRationale.c: It is the device MTU that is copied and the route MTU that is ignored, the opposite of this option.

questions.stem: How does DSR with IPIP dispatch differ from DSR with Geneve dispatch in terms of transporting the service IP/port to the backend?

options.text: IPIP does not rely on a Geneve option to transport the service IP/port; instead it encapsulates the original packet in an IPIP tunnel.
IPIP uses a Geneve option to carry the service IP/port, while Geneve uses an IP option.
IPIP uses Cilium-specific IP options to carry the service IP/port, while Geneve uses an IPv6 extension header.
IPIP and Geneve both rely on a Geneve option, but IPIP requires matching frontend and backend ports.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that compared to DSR mode with Geneve, the IPIP dispatch does not rely on a Geneve option to transport the service IP/port to the backend. Instead, it encapsulates the original client packet in an IPIP tunnel.

optionRationale.b: This reverses the roles: IPIP does not use a Geneve option; Geneve does.
optionRationale.c: Cilium-specific IP options are used by the IPv4 option / IPv6 extension header dispatch, not by IPIP.
optionRationale.d: IPIP does not rely on a Geneve option at all; the port matching requirement is separate.

questions.stem: An engineer needs per-packet latency reduced and is willing to accept up-front memory allocation for map entries. Which ConfigMap option should be set to `true`, and what must the engineer expect on the next Cilium startup?

optionRationale.b: `debug` concerns logging and visibility events, not map pre-allocation or latency.
optionRationale.c: `clean-cilium-state` removes all Cilium state irreversibly and is unrelated to latency optimisation.
optionRationale.d: `monitor-aggregation-interval` controls the tracing event reporting interval, not map pre-allocation.

It is replaced with a new service entry of type ClusterIP that includes all backend pods in the cluster.

optionRationale.c: The new entry is of type LocalRedirect, not ClusterIP, and is restricted to node-local backends.
