questions.stem: An engineer needs to redirect traffic that is destined for a Kubernetes Service. Which matcher is intended for that case, given the constraints on AddressMatcher?

options.text: addressMatcher, because it accepts any IP including Service frontends.
ServiceMatcher, because AddressMatcher is intended for IPs that do not belong to a Kubernetes Service.
addressMatchCIDRs, because it constrains clusterwide which Service addresses may be redirected.
localEndpointSelector, because it selects the Service whose traffic is redirected.

questions.explanation: AddressMatcher is intended for IPs that do not belong to a Kubernetes Service, and Cilium refuses to override a frontend owned by another Service. To redirect traffic destined for a Service, ServiceMatcher should be used instead.

optionRationale.a: AddressMatcher is explicitly not intended for Service IPs, and a coinciding ClusterIP frontend causes the policy not to be applied.
optionRationale.c: addressMatchCIDRs is a clusterwide Helm option that constrains allowed addresses; it is not a matcher for Service traffic.
optionRationale.d: localEndpointSelector selects backend pods, not the Service whose traffic is redirected.

citations.title: AddressMatcher
citations.quote:
To redirect traffic destined for a Service, use `ServiceMatcher`_
   instead.

questions.stem: An existing cluster is running kube-proxy as a DaemonSet. An engineer deletes the kube-proxy DaemonSet and its ConfigMap, then runs iptables-save | grep -v KUBE | iptables-restore on each node. What is the immediate consequence for service traffic?

options.text: Existing service connections will break and service-related traffic will stop until the Cilium replacement is installed.
Service traffic continues uninterrupted because Cilium automatically takes over.
Only new connections are affected; existing connections remain intact.
Service traffic is unaffected because kube-proxy operates independently of iptables.

questions.explanation: The excerpt explicitly warns that removing kube-proxy will break existing service connections and will also stop service-related traffic until the Cilium replacement has been installed.

optionRationale.b: Cilium is not yet installed; the excerpt states traffic stops until the replacement is installed.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt says existing connections will break, not just new ones.
optionRationale.d: kube-proxy relies on iptables rules; removing it affects service traffic.

citations.title: Quick-Start
citations.quote:
Be aware that removing ``kube-proxy`` will break existing service connections. It will also stop service related traffic
   until the Cilium replacement has been installed.

questions.stem: A platform team wants to use DSR with IPIP for a LoadBalancer service. Their Cilium installation is running in overlay mode. What is the outcome?

options.text: DSR with IPIP works, but only if the service frontend port equals the backend port.
DSR with IPIP does not work because it requires Cilium to be deployed in arch_direct_routing.
DSR with IPIP works because the IPIP tunnel provides the overlay encapsulation.
DSR with IPIP works only if bpf.lbModeAnnotation is set to true.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that DSR with IPIP requires Cilium to be deployed in arch_direct_routing and will not work in arch_overlay mode. Therefore, in overlay mode the feature cannot be used.

optionRationale.a: Matching frontend and backend ports is a prerequisite for IPIP, but it does not overcome the direct-routing requirement.
optionRationale.c: The IPIP tunnel is used to encapsulate traffic to the backend, but the excerpt explicitly says it will not work in arch_overlay mode.
optionRationale.d: bpf.lbModeAnnotation is needed for annotation-based DSR, but it does not change the requirement for arch_direct_routing.

citations.title: Direct Server Return (DSR) with IPIP
citations.quote:
It requires Cilium to be deployed in arch_direct_routing, it will not
work in arch_overlay mode.

questions.stem: An engineer configures an AddressMatcher rule that redirects traffic matching IP address 169.254.169.254 on Layer 4 port 8080 with protocol TCP. Which backend does the example redirect this traffic to?

options.text: A backend pod with labels app=proxy on Layer 4 port 80 with protocol TCP.
A backend pod with labels app=proxy on Layer 4 port 8080 with protocol TCP.
A backend pod with labels app=proxy on Layer 4 port 80 with protocol UDP.
A backend pod selected by localEndpointSelector app=proxy on port 169.254.

questions.explanation: The example redirects traffic matching IP address 169.254.169.254 and Layer 4 port 8080 with protocol TCP to a backend pod deployed with labels app=proxy and Layer 4 port 80 with protocol TCP. The localEndpointSelector set to app=proxy selects the backend pods where traffic is redirected to.

optionRationale.b: The backend port in the example is 80, not 8080; 8080 is the frontend port.
optionRationale.c: The protocol in the example is TCP, not UDP.
optionRationale.d: 169.254.169.254 is the frontend address, not a backend port, and the backend port is 80.

citations.title: AddressMatcher
citations.quote:
The example shows how to redirect from traffic matching, IP address ``169.254.169.254``
and Layer 4 port ``8080`` with protocol ``TCP``, to a backend pod deployed with
labels ``app=proxy`` and Layer 4 port ``80`` with protocol ``TCP``.

questions.stem: A CiliumLocalRedirectPolicy uses a serviceMatcher for a service that exposes multiple ports, and the engineer specifies several ports under toPorts in redirectFrontend. What must be true of those ports?

options.text: They must be named.
They must be numeric only.
They must match the backend pod container ports exactly.
They must be listed in the same order as the service ports.

questions.explanation: When multiple service ports are specified in the spec, they must be named. The port names are used to map frontend ports with backend ports.

optionRationale.b: The requirement is that the ports be named, not that they be numeric only.
optionRationale.c: The ports under redirectBackend must exist in the backend pod spec, but the frontend ports under redirectFrontend are not required to match container ports exactly.
optionRationale.d: There is no requirement about ordering; the requirement is that the ports be named.

citations.title: ServiceMatcher
citations.quote: Additionally, when multiple service ports are specified in the spec, they must be named.

questions.stem: After a serviceMatcher policy is applied, what replaces the existing service entry created by Cilium's eBPF kube-proxy replacement?

options.text: A new service entry of type LocalRedirect, which may only have node-local backend pods.
A new service entry of type ClusterIP with the same backends.
A new service entry of type NodePort with node-local backends.
The service entry is removed and traffic is dropped.

questions.explanation: Applying a policy of this type replaces the existing service entry with a new service entry of type LocalRedirect, and that entry may only have node-local backend pods.

optionRationale.b: The replacement type is LocalRedirect, not ClusterIP.
optionRationale.c: NodePort is not the replacement type described.
optionRationale.d: The entry is replaced, not removed.

citations.title: ServiceMatcher
citations.quote:
the existing service entry
created by Cilium's eBPF kube-proxy replacement will be replaced with a new
service entry of type ``LocalRedirect``. This entry may only have node-local backend pods.

questions.stem: An engineer is migrating a cluster from the 10.10.0.0/16 CIDR to 10.20.0.0/16. After updating the CiliumPodIPPool resource and restarting the Cilium operator, the engineer cordons Node Group 1 and drains it. What is the immediate consequence for the pods that were running on Node Group 1?

options.text: The pods are rescheduled to Node Group 2 and receive IP addresses from the new 10.20.0.0/16 CIDR.
The pods remain on Node Group 1 but are assigned new IP addresses from the 10.20.0.0/16 CIDR.
The pods are deleted and must be manually recreated to obtain IP addresses from the new pool.
The pods are rescheduled to Node Group 2 but retain their original IP addresses from the 10.10.0.0/16 CIDR.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that after draining Node Group 1, the nginx pod running on kind-worker (Node Group 1) is rescheduled on kind-control-plane (Node Group 2) with an IP address from the updated pool (10.20.11.182, which is within 10.20.0.0/16).

optionRationale.b: Incorrect because the nodes in Node Group 1 are cordoned and drained, so pods cannot remain on them.
optionRationale.c: Incorrect because the pods are rescheduled, not deleted and manually recreated.
optionRationale.d: Incorrect because the new pods receive IP addresses from the updated pool, not the old one.

citations.title: Updating existing CiliumPodIPPools
citations.quote: The nginx pod running on kind-worker is rescheduled on kind-control-plane with an IP address from the updated pool

questions.stem: An engineer assigns a weight annotation to an EndpointSlice that contributes four backend addresses to a Service. How does the configured weight apply?

options.text: It applies to all backends in that EndpointSlice.
It applies only to the first backend listed in the EndpointSlice.
It is divided evenly among the backends in the EndpointSlice.
It applies only to backends that have no other annotations.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that the configured weight applies to all backends in a given EndpointSlice, so every address in that slice shares the same weight.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt makes no distinction between the first and subsequent backends; the weight covers all of them.
optionRationale.c: The weight is not divided among backends; it applies to all backends in the slice.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says nothing about other annotations affecting whether the weight applies.

citations.title: Annotation-based Load Balancing Weight
citations.quote: The configured weight applies to all backends in a given ``EndpointSlice``.

questions.stem: Several subnets satisfy the VPC, Availability Zone and any configured ID or tag criteria. How does the operator choose between them?

options.text: It selects the subnet with the lowest ID in lexicographic order.
It selects the subnet with the most available addresses.
It selects the subnet that was created most recently.
It selects the subnet with the fewest existing ENIs attached.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that if multiple subnets match, the subnet with the most available addresses is selected.

optionRationale.a: No ordering by ID is mentioned; the selection criterion is address availability.
optionRationale.c: Creation time is not part of the described selection criteria.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt refers to available addresses, not to the number of attached ENIs.

citations.title: ENI Creation
citations.quote:
If multiple subnets match, the subnet with the most available addresses
is selected.

questions.stem: A security team wants to block traffic from a specific set of CIDRs while allowing all other traffic to a LoadBalancer service. How can this be achieved with Cilium?

options.text: Set service.cilium.io/src-ranges-policy: deny on the service and list the CIDRs in loadBalancerSourceRanges.
Set service.cilium.io/src-ranges-policy: allow and list the CIDRs in loadBalancerSourceRanges.
Set service.cilium.io/type: LoadBalancer and leave loadBalancerSourceRanges empty.
Enable bpf.lbSourceRangeAllTypes=true and list the CIDRs in loadBalancerSourceRanges.

questions.explanation: The excerpt explains that the list can be turned into a deny-list, blocking traffic from certain CIDRs while allowing everything else, through the service.cilium.io/src-ranges-policy annotation, which accepts allow or deny.

optionRationale.b: The allow value is the default allow-list behaviour, which permits only the listed CIDRs rather than blocking them.
optionRationale.c: The type annotation avoids creating corresponding NodePort and ClusterIP services; it does not invert the CIDR list.
optionRationale.d: That Helm option propagates the ranges to other service types; it does not change allow-list into deny-list.

citations.title: LoadBalancer Source Ranges Checks
citations.quote:
Cilium also supports the option to turn this list into a deny-list, in order
to block traffic from certain CIDRs while allowing everything else.

questions.stem: What does selecting loadBalancer.dsrDispatch=ipip automatically enable on backend nodes?

options.text: It enables Geneve encapsulation for service traffic.
It enables inbound IPIP termination on the backend nodes, stripping the outer header and delivering the inner packet to the local backend Pod.
It enables SNAT forwarding mode globally.
It enables the service.cilium.io/lb-algorithm annotation.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that selecting loadBalancer.dsrDispatch=ipip automatically enables the inbound IPIP termination on the backend nodes (stripping the outer header and delivering the inner packet to the local backend Pod), so no additional setting is required. The other options are incorrect: Geneve is a different dispatch mode, SNAT is a different forwarding mode, and the lb-algorithm annotation is enabled by a different setting (bpf.lbAlgorithmAnnotation=true).

optionRationale.a: Geneve is a different dispatch mode, not enabled by dsrDispatch=ipip.
optionRationale.c: SNAT is a different forwarding mode; dsrDispatch=ipip does not enable it globally.
optionRationale.d: The lb-algorithm annotation is enabled by bpf.lbAlgorithmAnnotation=true, not by dsrDispatch=ipip.

citations.title: Direct Server Return (DSR) with IPIP
citations.quote:
Selecting ``loadBalancer.dsrDispatch=ipip`` automatically enables the inbound IPIP
termination on the backend nodes (stripping the outer header and delivering the
inner packet to the local backend Pod), so no additional setting is required:

questions.stem: An engineer wants the operator-driven migration to create the multi-pool pool under a name other than default, configured globally in the same Helm upgrade that restarts the operator. Which setting accomplishes this?

options.text: --set ipam.operator.autoCreateCiliumPodIPPools.<name>.ipv4.cidrs, using the desired name as the key
--set-string extraConfig.ipam-default-ip-pool=<pool-name>
--set ipam.mode=<pool-name>
--set operator.rollOutPods=<pool-name>

questions.explanation: To use a different default pool name for the migration, the setting is configured globally in the same Helm upgrade that restarts the operator, using extraConfig.ipam-default-ip-pool with the desired pool name.

optionRationale.a: That key controls the CIDRs of an auto-created pool; it is not the documented way to choose the default pool name globally.
optionRationale.c: ipam.mode selects the IPAM mode, such as multi-pool, not the pool name.
optionRationale.d: operator.rollOutPods is a boolean controlling whether the operator pods are restarted.

citations.title: Practical Example
citations.quote:
If you want to use a different default pool name for the migration, configure
it globally in the same Helm upgrade that restarts the operator, with
``--set-string extraConfig.ipam-default-ip-pool=<pool-name>``.

questions.stem: When deploying the eBPF kube-proxy replacement in co-existence with kube-proxy on an already running cluster, what must be expected if the replacement is added or removed to delegate operation?

options.text: Existing connections will break because the NAT tables are not aware of each other.
Existing connections will be preserved because both mechanisms synchronise their NAT tables.
Only new connections will be affected; existing connections remain intact.
The cluster will automatically reboot nodes to apply the change.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that when deploying the eBPF kube-proxy replacement under co-existence with kube-proxy, both mechanisms operate independently. If the replacement is added or removed on an already running cluster, existing connections will break because the NAT tables are not aware of each other.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says the NAT tables are not aware of each other, so they do not synchronise.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt says existing connections will break, not just new ones.
optionRationale.d: Node reboots are not mentioned in the excerpt.

citations.title: Quick-Start
citations.quote:
if the eBPF kube-proxy replacement is added or removed on an already
   *running* cluster in order to delegate operation from respectively back to kube-proxy,
   then it must be expected that existing connections will break since, for example,
   both NAT tables are not aware of each other.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the default interpretation of loadBalancerSourceRanges in Cilium?

options.text: It specifies an allow-list of CIDRs, so traffic not originating from those CIDRs is automatically dropped.
It specifies a deny-list of CIDRs, so traffic from those CIDRs is dropped and everything else is allowed.
It specifies a list of CIDRs that are exempt from all Cilium policy enforcement.
It specifies a list of CIDRs that are only used for NodePort services.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that loadBalancerSourceRanges by default specifies an allow-list of CIDRs, meaning traffic originating not from those CIDRs is automatically dropped.

optionRationale.b: Deny-list behaviour is opt-in via the service.cilium.io/src-ranges-policy: deny annotation, not the default.
optionRationale.c: The field filters traffic by source IP; it does not exempt CIDRs from policy enforcement.
optionRationale.d: By default the CIDRs apply to the LoadBalancer service, not to the corresponding NodePort service.

citations.title: LoadBalancer Source Ranges Checks
citations.quote:
The ``loadBalancerSourceRanges`` by default specifies an allow-list of CIDRs,
meaning, traffic originating not from those CIDRs is automatically dropped.

questions.stem: An engineer enables XDP acceleration for NodePort handling and then tries to observe the packets that were pushed back out of the device for NodePort handling right at the XDP layer. Why does `tcpdump` not show them, and what should be used instead?

options.text: The packets are encrypted before the XDP layer, so only `cilium-dbg status` can show them.
The packets never reach the device, so only the Kubernetes API server can show them.
Packet taps come at a much later stage in the networking stack, so Cilium's monitor command or metric counters should be used instead.
The packets are only visible when `loadBalancer.acceleration` is set to `disabled`, so the setting must be turned off first.

questions.explanation: The excerpt notes that packets pushed back out of the device for NodePort handling right at the XDP layer are not visible in tcpdump because packet taps come at a much later stage in the networking stack, and that Cilium's monitor command or metric counters can be used instead for visibility.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt attributes the invisibility to the position of packet taps in the stack, not to encryption, and does not mention `cilium-dbg status` as a packet-visibility tool.
optionRationale.b: The excerpt says the packets are pushed back out of the device, so they do reach it; it recommends the monitor command or metric counters, not the API server.
optionRationale.d: Disabling the acceleration is not presented as a way to gain visibility; the excerpt recommends the monitor command or metric counters.

citations.title: LoadBalancer & NodePort XDP Acceleration
citations.quote:
Note that packets which have been pushed back out of the device for NodePort handling
right at the XDP layer are not visible in tcpdump since packet taps come at a much
later stage in the networking stack.

questions.stem: After pods have been evicted from a node group during a pool CIDR migration, what must be done for that node group before it is uncordoned?

options.text: Delete the `CiliumNodes` for the node group and restart the Cilium agents running on it.
Delete the `CiliumPodIPPool` and recreate it with the new CIDR.
Restart the Cilium operator and re-apply the pool manifest.
Drain the node group a second time with `--ignore-daemonsets`.

questions.explanation: The procedure for each node group is to delete the `CiliumNodes` for that group, restart the Cilium agents running on it, and then uncordon it.

optionRationale.b: The pool is updated once at the start; it is not deleted and recreated per node group.
optionRationale.c: Restarting the operator is an earlier step, performed once after the pool update.
optionRationale.d: Draining is done once per node group before the `CiliumNodes` are deleted and the agents restarted.

citations.title: Updating existing CiliumPodIPPools
citations.quote: 4. Delete ``CiliumNodes`` for Node Group 1, restart the Cilium agents running on Node Group 1 and uncordon Node Group 1.

questions.stem: A Service is backed by two EndpointSlices with weights `70` and `30`. Later, the second EndpointSlice is changed from weight `30` to weight `0`. What is the effect on traffic?

options.text: The second slice's backends are removed immediately and existing connections are reset.
The second slice's backends enter maintenance: existing connections continue, but new traffic goes entirely to the first slice.
The weight `0` is treated as invalid and ignored, so the split stays 70/30.
New traffic is split evenly between both slices.

questions.explanation: A weight of `0` marks those backends as being in maintenance so that existing connections can continue while new traffic is steered to other backends. The excerpt confirms the first slice then receives 100% of the new traffic share.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt says existing connections can continue, not that they are reset.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt says invalid values are ignored, but `0` is a valid value with a defined maintenance meaning.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt states new traffic is steered entirely to the remaining non-maintenance backends.

citations.title: Annotation-based Load Balancing Weight
citations.quote:
A weight of ``0`` marks those
backends as being in maintenance so that existing connections can continue
while new traffic is steered to other backends.

questions.stem: A CiliumLocalRedirectPolicy uses an addressMatcher frontend and specifies several ports under toPorts. What must be done with those frontend ports?

options.text: They must be named, and the port names are used to map frontend ports with backend ports.
They must be listed in ascending numeric order.
They must each be repeated under redirectBackend with the same numbers.
They must be expressed as a single port range.

questions.explanation: When multiple ports are specified for frontend in toPorts, the ports need to be named, and the port names are used to map frontend ports with backend ports.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt requires naming, not a particular ordering.
optionRationale.c: The requirement stated is that the ports in toPorts under redirectBackend exist in the backend pod spec, not that frontend ports be repeated.
optionRationale.d: No port-range form is described; the requirement is that the ports be named.

citations.title: AddressMatcher
citations.quote:
When multiple ports are specified for frontend in ``toPorts``, the ports need
to be named. The port names will be used to map frontend ports with backend ports.

questions.stem: What is the effect of leaving spec.loadBalancerSourceRanges empty on a LoadBalancer service?

options.text: No restrictions on access are applied.
All external traffic is dropped.
Only in-cluster traffic is allowed.
The service is not programmed by the kube-proxy replacement.

questions.explanation: If the field is empty, no restrictions for access will be applied.

optionRationale.b: An empty list does not drop traffic; it applies no restrictions.
optionRationale.c: In-cluster traffic is always allowed regardless of the field.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt does not state that an empty field prevents programming.

citations.title: LoadBalancer Source Ranges Checks
citations.quote: If the field is empty, no restrictions for the access will be applied.

questions.stem: A LoadBalancer service has spec.loadBalancerSourceRanges set to 192.168.1.0/24. By default, which services does this CIDR restriction apply to?

options.text: Only the LoadBalancer service, not the corresponding NodePort or ClusterIP services.
The LoadBalancer service and its corresponding NodePort service, but not ClusterIP.
All service types created for the service, including NodePort and ClusterIP.
Only the ClusterIP service, because NodePort and LoadBalancer are externally exposed.

questions.explanation: By default the white-listed CIDRs in spec.loadBalancerSourceRanges apply only to the LoadBalancer service, not to the NodePort or ClusterIP services that are installed alongside it.

optionRationale.b: The restriction does not extend to NodePort by default.
optionRationale.c: Propagating to all externally exposed types requires the Helm option bpf.lbSourceRangeAllTypes=true.
optionRationale.d: The restriction applies to the LoadBalancer service, not the ClusterIP service.

citations.title: LoadBalancer Source Ranges Checks
citations.quote: By default the specified white-listed CIDRs in ``spec.loadBalancerSourceRanges`` only apply to the ``LoadBalancer`` service, but not the corresponding ``NodePort`` or ``ClusterIP`` service which get installed along with the ``LoadBalancer`` service.

questions.stem: Which Helm values are required to opt into DSR IPIP on a per-service basis through the service.cilium.io/forwarding-mode: dsr annotation while keeping the global default forwarding mode as SNAT?

options.text: bpf.lbModeAnnotation=true and loadBalancer.dsrDispatch=ipip
loadBalancer.mode=dsr and loadBalancer.dsrDispatch=geneve
bpf.lbAlgorithmAnnotation=true only
loadBalancer.dsrDispatch=ipip only, without bpf.lbModeAnnotation

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that annotation-based DSR and SNAT mode requires bpf.lbModeAnnotation=true together with an explicit loadBalancer.dsrDispatch=ipip to define how the per-service DSR packets are dispatched to backends.

optionRationale.b: The example keeps loadBalancer.mode=snat and uses dsrDispatch=ipip, not geneve.
optionRationale.c: bpf.lbAlgorithmAnnotation=true is for annotation-based load balancing algorithm selection, not for enabling DSR mode.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says bpf.lbModeAnnotation=true is required together with loadBalancer.dsrDispatch=ipip.

citations.title: Direct Server Return (DSR) with IPIP
citations.quote:
this requires
``bpf.lbModeAnnotation=true`` together with an explicit
``loadBalancer.dsrDispatch=ipip`` to define how the per-service DSR packets are
dispatched to backends.

questions.stem: Several subnets satisfy the VPC ID and Availability Zone criteria, and no `subnet-ids` or `subnet-tags` are configured. The operator has already failed to place the ENI in the node's own subnet and in a subnet sharing its route table. Which subnet does it choose next?

options.text: The subnet with the most available addresses among those matching VPC and Availability Zone.
The subnet with the fewest available addresses among those matching VPC and Availability Zone.
The first subnet returned by the AWS API that matches VPC and Availability Zone.
No ENI is created; allocation fails once the node subnet and route-table options are exhausted.

questions.explanation: After the node-subnet and route-table attempts fail, the operator falls back to the largest subnet matching VPC and Availability Zone, and elsewhere the excerpt says the subnet with the most available addresses is selected when multiple match.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt selects the subnet with the most available addresses, not the fewest.
optionRationale.c: There is no first-returned rule; selection is by available addresses.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt describes a fallback rather than a failure at this point.

citations.title: ENI Creation
citations.quote:
If this is not possible, it will fall back to
creating the ENI in the largest subnet matching VPC and Availability Zone.

questions.stem: You are migrating a kind cluster from cluster-pool IPAM to multi-pool IPAM. The Helm upgrade has switched ipam.mode to multi-pool, enabled the operator migration, and restarted only the Cilium operator. You then delete the Cilium agent pod on kind-worker. After it restarts, what should you expect for that node?

options.text: The agent runs in multi-pool IPAM mode, requests IPs from the default pool, and preserves the IPs of restored endpoints.
The agent remains in cluster-pool mode until every other agent has been restarted, and continues using its existing cluster-pool allocation.
The agent runs in multi-pool mode but all existing endpoints on the node are recreated with new IPs from the default pool.
The agent runs in multi-pool mode and requests IPs from a pool named after the node, because the default pool is only used by the operator.

questions.explanation: After the agent restarts, it runs in multi-pool IPAM mode and requests IPs from the default pool while preserving the IPs of restored endpoints. Other agents may still be in cluster-pool mode until they are restarted, but this restarted agent has moved to multi-pool.

optionRationale.b: A restarted agent moves to multi-pool mode; it does not wait for every other agent to be restarted before changing mode.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt states that the restarted agent preserves the IPs of restored endpoints, so existing endpoints are not all recreated with new IPs.
optionRationale.d: The restarted agent requests IPs from the default pool, not from a pool named after the node.

citations.title: Practical Example
citations.quote:
After the agent restarts, it runs in multi-pool IPAM mode and requests IPs from
the default pool while preserving the IPs of restored endpoints:

questions.stem: A cluster uses DSR mode. Because a given backend can serve multiple services, the backend must know which service IP/port to use as the source when replying. How does Cilium convey this, and what is the cost?

options.text: It encodes the information into the packet using a dispatch mechanism, at the cost of advertising a lower MTU.
It performs reverse SNAT on the node that received the request, at no cost to the MTU.
It sets bpf.disableExternalIPMitigation to true, at the cost of losing client source IP preservation.
It relies on the cloud provider's source/destination IP address checking to supply the service IP/port.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that Cilium encodes the service IP/port information into the packet using one of the dispatch mechanisms, at the cost of advertising a lower MTU.

optionRationale.b: Reverse SNAT on the receiving node is the SNAT mode behaviour that DSR avoids, and it is not how the service IP/port is conveyed.
optionRationale.c: That flag concerns the ExternalIP mitigation for CVE-2020-8554 and does not encode service information.
optionRationale.d: Cloud address checking must in some environments be disabled for DSR to work; it does not supply the service IP/port.

citations.title: Direct Server Return (DSR)
citations.quote: Cilium encodes this information into the packet (using one of the dispatch mechanisms described below), at the cost of advertising a lower MTU.

questions.stem: On a node, the configured NodePort range overlaps with the ephemeral port range net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range. What does Cilium do by default, and why?

options.text: It appends the NodePort range to net.ipv4.ip_local_reserved_ports, to prevent a NodePort service from hijacking traffic of a host local application whose source port matches the service port.
It shrinks the ephemeral port range so that the two ranges no longer overlap.
It refuses to start the Cilium agent until the overlap is removed manually.
It disables NodePort services on that node until the overlap is resolved.

questions.explanation: The excerpt says that if the NodePort port range overlaps with the ephemeral port range, Cilium will append the NodePort range to the reserved ports, which is needed to prevent a NodePort service from hijacking traffic of a host local application whose source port matches the service port.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt describes appending to the reserved ports, not modifying the ephemeral port range itself.
optionRationale.c: No such refusal is described; the excerpt describes an automatic modification of the reserved ports.
optionRationale.d: NodePort services are not disabled; the protection is applied through the reserved ports list.

citations.title: NodePort Devices, Port and Bind settings
citations.quote:
If the NodePort port range overlaps with the ephemeral port range
(``net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range``), Cilium will append the NodePort range to
the reserved ports (``net.ipv4.ip_local_reserved_ports``).

questions.stem: A Service is backed by two EndpointSlice objects with weights 70 and 30. Later, the operator changes the second EndpointSlice from weight 30 to weight 0. What is the effect on traffic?

options.text: The weight 0 is treated as invalid and ignored, so traffic continues at roughly 70/30.
The second slice's backends are removed immediately and all existing connections to them are terminated.
The second slice's backends enter maintenance: existing connections can continue, but new traffic goes entirely to the first slice's backends.
New traffic is split evenly between the two slices because a zero weight resets the distribution.

questions.explanation: The excerpt explains that a weight of 0 marks those backends as being in maintenance so that existing connections can continue while new traffic is steered to other backends. When the second slice is changed to 0, the first slice receives 100% of the new traffic share.

optionRationale.c: authSecretRef references the name of a secret in the BGP secrets namespace; the namespace is not part of the reference.

Immediately after the label change.
Immediately after the BGP Control Plane sends a BGP Notification to the peer.
Only after the node is shut down and the TCP session times out.

optionRationale.c: The BGP Control Plane sends a Notification when the node is unselected only if the peer does not support Graceful Restart with Notification; here the peer does support it, so the Stale Timer applies.
optionRationale.d: The withdrawal is driven by the Stale Timer, not by TCP session timeout after shutdown.

The excerpt also notes that none is the default and means no preference, while remote prefers remote endpoints.

optionRationale.c: The excerpt defines local as preferring endpoints from the local cluster if available, not as avoiding the local cluster.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt explicitly allows remote endpoints if and only if all local backends are not available or unhealthy.

questions.stem: Two clusters export Services with the same name and namespace, but they disagree on the SessionAffinity property. What does Cilium do?

questions.stem: A platform team wants Cilium to drop traffic destined for addresses that are not valid endpoints, and to do so as early as possible for maximum performance. Which Cilium datapath object should they rely on, and which hook does it use?

The endpoint policy object, which maps packets to identities and enforces L3/L4 policy.

optionRationale.c: The endpoint policy object is described as the primary object responsible for mapping packets to identities and enforcing L3 and L4 policies, not as the XDP prefilter that drops traffic to non-endpoint destinations.
optionRationale.d: The socket operations hook is attached to a cgroup and runs on TCP events to monitor state transitions; it is not the XDP-based prefilter object.

questions.stem: A platform team wants Cilium to drop malicious or unexpected traffic as early as possible, before the networking stack has done any other processing, and to achieve the best possible packet processing performance. Which BPF hook should the team use for this filtering?

questions.explanation: The XDP hook is the correct choice. The excerpt states that it is at the earliest point possible in the networking driver and triggers a run of the BPF program upon packet reception. This achieves the best possible packet processing performance because the program runs directly on the packet data before any other processing can happen, and the hook is ideal for filtering programs that drop malicious or unexpected traffic and other common DDOS protection mechanisms.

optionRationale.b: The Traffic Control Ingress/Egress hook is attached to a networking interface, same as XDP, but it runs after the networking stack has done initial processing of the packet, so it is not the earliest point described for dropping traffic before other processing.
optionRationale.c: The Socket operations hook is attached to a specific cgroup and runs on TCP events; it is not the packet-reception hook in the networking driver used for early filtering.
optionRationale.d: The Socket send/recv hook runs on every send operation performed by a TCP socket; it is not the hook for dropping traffic at packet reception before stack processing.

questions.stem: An engineer changes the label patterns in the `cilium-config` ConfigMap and restarts the Cilium pod on the node where a workload is running. What happens to that workload's existing identity?

questions.stem: An engineer is debugging an Ingress issue and wants to verify if the request is reaching the Envoy proxy. They identify the proxy port from the Cilium logs as 19672. What command should they run on the node to test this specific port?

options.text: `curl -v http://localhost:19672`
`curl -v http://localhost:31911`
`kubectl exec -n kube-system ds/cilium -- hubble observe -f --identity 2`
`kubectl get service cilium-ingress-basic-ingress`

questions.explanation: The excerpt provides a scenario where the proxy port is identified as 19672 from the logs. It then shows the command `curl -v http://localhost:19672` to send a request directly to the Envoy proxy port on the node.

optionRationale.b: Port 31911 is the node port for the LoadBalancer service, not the direct Envoy proxy port identified in this specific scenario (19672).
optionRationale.c: This command is used to observe flows, not to send a test request to a specific port to verify connectivity to the proxy.
optionRationale.d: This command retrieves service information but does not test the connectivity to the specific proxy port.

citations.title: Connectivity Troubleshooting
citations.quote:
# After ssh to any of k8s node, send request to Envoy proxy port directly
     $ curl -v  http://localhost:19672

questions.stem: You apply a policy that restricts deathstar landing requests to ships carrying the label org=empire. You then run a landing request from a tiefighter pod, which has that label. What is the expected result?

options.text: The request hangs and must be killed with Control-C.
The request is rejected with a connection refused error.
The request succeeds and returns 'Ship landed'.
The request succeeds only after the policy is deleted.

questions.explanation: The excerpt shows that after applying the policy, only the tiefighter pods with the org=empire label succeed, and the sample output for the tiefighter request is 'Ship landed'.

optionRationale.a: The hanging behaviour is described for the xwing request, not the labelled tiefighter.
optionRationale.b: The excerpt does not describe a connection refused error; the blocked request hangs instead.
optionRationale.d: The tiefighter request succeeds with the policy in place, as shown in the sample session.

citations.title: Apply an L3/L4 Policy
citations.quote: Now if we run the landing requests again, only the *tiefighter* pods with the label ``org=empire`` will succeed.

questions.stem: During a Cilium installation on a small cluster of 5 nodes, an engineer considers disabling endpoint health checking entirely with --set endpointHealthChecking.enabled=false and --set healthChecking=false. What does the guidance recommend?

options.text: Keep those features enabled initially on a smaller cluster (3-10 nodes) to detect potential packet loss due to firewall rules or hypervisor settings.
Disable them immediately because they are not needed on clusters with fewer than 10 nodes.
Disable them only if the cluster has more than 1000 nodes.
Enable them only when using a cloud provider with pod CIDR allocation.

questions.explanation: Although the flags disable endpoint health checking entirely, the recommendation is to enable those features initially on a smaller cluster (3-10 nodes) where they can be used to detect potential packet loss due to firewall rules or hypervisor settings.

optionRationale.b: The guidance recommends the opposite: keep them enabled initially on small clusters.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt does not link disabling to cluster size above 1000 nodes; it recommends enabling on 3-10 nodes.
optionRationale.d: Pod CIDR allocation relates to ipam.mode=kubernetes, not to health checking.

citations.title: Setup
citations.quote: However it is recommended that those features be enabled initially on a smaller cluster (3-10 nodes) where it can be used to detect potential packet loss due to firewall rules or hypervisor settings.

questions.stem: An engineer deploys the cilium-pre-flight-check Deployment in kube-system ahead of an upgrade. After waiting, `kubectl get deployment -n kube-system cilium-pre-flight-check` shows READY 0/1. What does the guidance say the engineer should do next?

options.text: Check the pod logs, for example with `kubectl logs -n kube-system deployment/cilium-pre-flight-check -c cnp-validator --previous`.
Proceed with the upgrade, because the pre-flight check only reports on policy formatting and does not block the upgrade.
Delete the Deployment and reinstall it, since a READY 0/1 state means the CNP Validator cannot be run at all.
Edit every CiliumNetworkPolicy in the cluster to remove its `.spec.labels` field before retrying.

questions.explanation: The guidance is to check whether the Deployment shows READY 1/1 and, if it does not, to check the pod logs. The sample logs are retrieved from the `cnp-validator` container of the Deployment, and the `--previous` flag is used in the example.

optionRationale.b: The text stresses the importance of running the validation before an upgrade, so proceeding regardless is contrary to the guidance.
optionRationale.c: Nothing in the guidance says a READY 0/1 state means the validator cannot run; the instruction is to inspect the pod logs.
optionRationale.d: Removing `.spec.labels` from every policy is not the prescribed step; the fix described is to correct the format of the labels on the invalid policy.

citations.title: CNP Validation
citations.quote:
Start by deployment the ``cilium-pre-flight-check`` and check if the
``Deployment`` shows READY 1/1, if it does not check the pod logs.

questions.stem: An engineer sets a custom list of label patterns in the Cilium ConfigMap, where the `labels` value is a space-separated string of regular expressions. What is the effect of this setting on the default list of label patterns?

options.text: The custom list replaces the default list entirely.
The custom list is appended to the default list of label patterns.
The custom list is ignored unless the `label-prefix-file` flag is also set.
The custom list is applied only to newly created identities, replacing the defaults for those identities.

questions.explanation: Upon defining a custom list of label patterns in the ConfigMap, Cilium adds the provided list of label patterns to the default list of label patterns. The configuration appends to the defaults rather than overriding them.

optionRationale.a: The custom list does not override the default set; it is added to it.
optionRationale.c: The `label-prefix-file` flag is mentioned as an alternative for declarative configuration of the exact set of prefixes, not as a condition for the ConfigMap setting to take effect.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt states that existing identities will not change as a result of the new configuration, and it does not describe the custom list as replacing defaults for new identities.

citations.title: Configuring Identity-Relevant Labels
citations.quote:
Upon defining a custom list of label patterns in the ConfigMap, Cilium adds the
provided list of label patterns to the default list of label patterns.

questions.stem: Which statement describes how the CNP Validator is invoked during a Cilium upgrade?

options.text: It is automatically executed as part of the pre-flight check pre_flight.
It must be run manually as a separate command after the upgrade has completed.
It runs only when a CiliumNetworkPolicy is first created, never during an upgrade.
It is triggered by the cleanup_preflight_check step at the end of the upgrade.

questions.explanation: The CNP Validator is automatically executed as part of the pre-flight check pre_flight, which is why running the validation before an upgrade is tied to that check.

optionRationale.b: The validator is part of the pre-flight check, not a manual post-upgrade step.
optionRationale.c: The validator is described as part of the pre-flight check for upgrades, not as a creation-time hook.
optionRationale.d: cleanup_preflight_check is mentioned as the step to continue with once policies are valid, not as the trigger for validation.

citations.title: CNP Validation
citations.quote:
This CNP Validator is
automatically executed as part of the pre-flight check pre_flight.

questions.stem: A platform team runs Cilium on a cluster whose nodes are protected by a firewall that blocks both ICMP Type 0/8 and TCP 4240 between nodes. What is the consequence for Cilium?

options.text: Cilium will still operate fine but will not be able to provide health information.
Cilium will fail to start on the nodes until one of the two methods is permitted.
Cilium will operate, but only if IPsec is enabled to carry the health traffic instead.
Cilium will fall back to using UDP 8472 for health monitoring.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that if the firewall permits neither of the two health-monitoring methods, Cilium still operates but cannot provide health information. Health monitoring is described as recommended but optional, so blocking it does not stop Cilium from working.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says Cilium will still operate fine, so a startup failure is not implied.
optionRationale.c: IPsec is mentioned only in relation to allowing ESP traffic through the firewall, not as a fallback for health checks.
optionRationale.d: UDP 8472 is the VXLAN overlay port, not a health-monitoring fallback.

citations.title: Firewall Rules
citations.quote:
If the firewall does not permit either of these
methods, Cilium will still operate fine but will not be able to provide health
information.

questions.stem: An engineer adds the label pattern `example\.com` to the `labels` setting in the `cilium-config` ConfigMap. Which labels will this pattern match?

options.text: Only labels whose key is exactly `example.com`.
Labels that start with `example.com`, because label patterns are implicitly anchored at the start of the label.
Labels that contain `example.com` anywhere in the key.
Labels that end with `example.com`.

questions.explanation: Label patterns are regular expressions that are implicitly anchored at the start of the label, so `example\.com` matches labels starting with `example.com`. To match the substring anywhere, the pattern would need a leading `.*`.

optionRationale.a: An exact match of the key requires an explicit end anchor such as `kind$` or `^kind$`.
optionRationale.c: Matching anywhere requires a leading `.*`, as in `.*example\.com`.
optionRationale.d: The implicit anchoring is at the start, not the end, of the label.

citations.title: Configuring Identity-Relevant Labels
citations.quote:
Label patterns are regular expressions that are implicitly anchored at the
start of the label. For example ``example\.com`` will match labels that start
with ``example.com``, whereas ``.*example\.com`` will match labels that contain
``example.com`` anywhere.

questions.stem: A cluster uses Cilium with IPsec enabled, and the nodes sit behind AWS Security Groups. What must the engineer ensure regarding the firewall?

options.text: The firewall must allow ESP traffic through, because AWS Security Groups do not allow ESP traffic by default.
The firewall must allow UDP 51871, because that is the IPsec tunnel endpoint port.
The firewall must allow UDP 8472, because IPsec is carried inside the VXLAN overlay.
No additional rules are needed, because AWS Security Groups permit ESP traffic by default.

questions.explanation: For IPsec-enabled deployments the excerpt requires the firewall to allow ESP traffic, and gives AWS Security Groups as an example of a firewall that does not allow ESP by default.

optionRationale.b: UDP 51871 is specified for WireGuard, not for IPsec.
optionRationale.c: UDP 8472 is the VXLAN overlay port and is not described as carrying IPsec.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says the opposite: AWS Security Groups do not allow ESP traffic by default.

citations.title: Firewall Rules
citations.quote:
For IPsec enabled Cilium deployments, you need to ensure that the firewall
allows ESP traffic through.

questions.stem: A team is evaluating how many request/response messages per second can be transmitted over a single TCP connection and over 32 parallel TCP connections. Which benchmark metric answers this?

options.text: Request/Response Rate
Throughput
Connections Rate
Connection churn

questions.explanation: Request/Response Rate is the number of request/response messages per second that can be transmitted over a single TCP connection and over 32 parallel TCP connections.

optionRationale.b: Throughput measures transfer rate, not messages per second.
optionRationale.c: Connections Rate measures connections established per second, not messages on existing connections.
optionRationale.d: Connection churn is not a metric described in the excerpt.

citations.title: Introduction
citations.quote:
The number of request/response messages per second that can be transmitted over
  a single TCP connection and over 32 parallel TCP connections.

questions.stem: You are defining a security policy for the Star Wars demo and want it to apply to the deathstar pods no matter which node they are scheduled on or when they are started. What does Cilium use to identify the pods the policy applies to?

options.text: The endpoint IP addresses of the pods
The labels assigned to the pods
The Kubernetes namespace of the pods
The node hostname the pods are running on

questions.explanation: Cilium applies policies based on pod labels, so the policy reaches the right pods irrespective of where or when they run in the cluster. Endpoint IP addresses are explicitly described as irrelevant for defining security policies.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt states that endpoint IP addresses are irrelevant when defining security policies.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt does not mention namespaces as the selection mechanism; it describes label-based selection.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says policies apply irrespective of where the pod is running, so node hostname is not the mechanism.

citations.title: Apply an L3/L4 Policy
citations.quote:
endpoint IP addresses are irrelevant when defining security
policies. Instead, you can use the labels assigned to the pods to define
security policies.

questions.stem: A Cilium agent's status output shows that the heartbeat key has not been updated in time, and this has now happened on three consecutive checks. What does Cilium conclude?

options.text: The quorum check is declared to have failed and Cilium is declared unhealthy.
The etcd cluster elects a new leader and the agent continues without any status change.
Cilium reports failure in cilium-dbg status and is restarted by the Kubernetes probes.
The agent stops watching the heartbeat key until the operator rewrites it.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that if the heartbeat key is not updated in time, the quorum check is declared to have failed and Cilium is declared unhealthy after 3 or more consecutive failures. The three-consecutive-failure threshold is therefore met.

optionRationale.b: Leader election and failover are how etcd itself handles an unhealthy endpoint; they are not the conclusion Cilium draws from a missed heartbeat.
optionRationale.c: Reporting failure in cilium-dbg status and being restarted by the probes is what happens when no etcd endpoints can be reached, not the heartbeat-based quorum check.
optionRationale.d: Agents watch the heartbeat key to validate their ability to receive key updates; the excerpt gives no behaviour of ceasing to watch it.

citations.title: Recovery behavior
citations.quote: If the heartbeat key is not updated in time, the quorum check is declared to have failed and Cilium is declared unhealthy after 3 or more consecutive failures.

questions.stem: A cluster uses Cilium in VXLAN overlay network mode on Linux hosts that have not been reconfigured from the default. Which UDP port must be open among all nodes to enable the overlay?

options.text: UDP 8472
UDP 6081
TCP 4240

questions.explanation: In VXLAN overlay mode, Cilium uses Linux's default VXLAN port 8472 over UDP unless Linux has been configured otherwise, and that port must be open among all nodes.

optionRationale.b: UDP 6081 is the port used by Geneve overlay mode, not VXLAN.
optionRationale.c: UDP 51871 is the WireGuard encryption tunnel endpoint.
optionRationale.d: TCP 4240 is for cilium-health monitoring, not the overlay.

citations.title: Firewall Rules
citations.quote: If you are using VXLAN overlay network mode, Cilium uses Linux's default VXLAN port 8472 over UDP, unless Linux has been configured otherwise.

questions.stem: A benchmark measures the number of connections per second that can be established in sequence, with a single request/response payload message transmitted for each new connection, testing both a single process and 32 parallel processes. Which metric is this?

options.text: Connections Rate
Throughput
Request/Response Rate
Packet drop rate

questions.explanation: Connections Rate is the number of connections per second established in sequence with a single request/response payload message per new connection, tested with a single process and 32 parallel processes.

optionRationale.b: Throughput concerns transfer rate over established connections.
optionRationale.c: Request/Response Rate concerns messages per second, not connection establishment.
optionRationale.d: Packet drop rate is not among the reported metrics.

citations.title: Introduction
citations.quote:
The number of connections per second that can be established in sequence with
  a single request/response payload message transmitted for each new connection.

questions.stem: An engineer is preparing a Helm values file for a large Cilium installation and wants to disable endpoint health checking entirely. Which pair of Helm settings accomplishes this?

options.text: Set endpointHealthChecking.enabled=false and healthChecking=false.
Set endpointHealthChecking.enabled=true and healthChecking=false.
Set endpointHealthChecking.enabled=false and healthChecking=true.
Set endpointHealthChecking.enabled=true and healthChecking=true.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that setting both endpointHealthChecking.enabled=false and healthChecking=false disables endpoint health checking entirely. Setting either to true would leave some health checking active.

optionRationale.b: endpointHealthChecking.enabled=true leaves endpoint health checking enabled, so it is not disabled entirely.
optionRationale.c: healthChecking=true leaves health checking enabled, so it is not disabled entirely.
optionRationale.d: Both settings are true, which enables rather than disables health checking.

citations.title: Setup
citations.quote:
``--set endpointHealthChecking.enabled=false`` and
  ``--set healthChecking=false`` disable endpoint health
  checking entirely.

questions.stem: In the sample pod listing from the cilium-test namespace, what do the readiness and liveness gates indicate?

options.text: The connectivity variant that is being exercised.
The success or failure of the test.
The number of network policies applied to the pod.
Whether the pod is scheduled on the host network.

questions.explanation: The excerpt explains that the pod name indicates the connectivity variant, while the readiness and liveness gate indicates success or failure of the test.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt assigns the connectivity variant to the pod name, not to the readiness and liveness gate.
optionRationale.c: The number of network policies is not what the readiness and liveness gate indicates according to the excerpt.
optionRationale.d: Host-network scheduling is not mentioned in the excerpt in connection with the readiness and liveness gate.

citations.title: Cilium connectivity tests
citations.quote:
The pod name indicates the connectivity
variant and the readiness and liveness gate indicates success or failure of the
test

questions.stem: An engineer is preparing firewall rules for a Cilium cluster that uses WireGuard encryption. Which port and protocol must be allowed?

options.text: UDP port 51871
UDP port 8472
TCP port 4240
UDP port 6081

questions.explanation: For WireGuard, the firewall must allow UDP port 51871, which is the WireGuard encryption tunnel endpoint.

optionRationale.b: UDP 8472 is the default VXLAN overlay port, not the WireGuard port.
optionRationale.c: TCP 4240 is used for cilium-health monitoring, not WireGuard.
optionRationale.d: UDP 6081 is the Geneve overlay port, not the WireGuard port.

citations.title: Firewall Rules
citations.quote: If you are using WireGuard, you must allow UDP port 51871.

questions.stem: During troubleshooting, an engineer runs `kubectl get cec cilium-ingress-default-basic-ingress -o json` and inspects the EDS resources. What naming convention is used for the Envoy Discovery Service (EDS) name?

options.text: `<namespace>/<service-name>:<port>`
`<service-name>-<namespace>-<port>`
`<ingress-name>-<proxy-port>`
`<cluster-ip>:<node-port>`

questions.explanation: The excerpt states: 'The Envoy Discovery Service (EDS) has a name that follows the convention `<namespace>/<service-name>:<port>`.' The example JSON shows names like `default/details:9080` and `default/productpage:9080`, which fit this pattern.

optionRationale.b: This format is not mentioned in the excerpt. The example `default/details:9080` clearly uses a slash and a colon.
optionRationale.c: This resembles the proxy port rule name (`cilium-ingress-default-basic-ingress:19672`) but is not the EDS naming convention.
optionRationale.d: This resembles the service IP and port format but is not the EDS naming convention described.

citations.title: Connectivity Troubleshooting
citations.quote: The Envoy Discovery Service (EDS) has a name that follows the convention ``<namespace>/<service-name>:<port>``.

questions.stem: A team is deploying Cilium on a new 5-node cluster and is deciding whether to disable endpoint health checking from the start. What does the guidance recommend?

options.text: Disable endpoint health checking immediately to reduce overhead on all cluster sizes.
Enable endpoint health checking initially on the smaller cluster so it can detect potential packet loss due to firewall rules or hypervisor settings.
Enable endpoint health checking only after the cluster grows beyond 10 nodes.
Endpoint health checking should never be enabled because it interferes with kube-proxy.

questions.explanation: The excerpt recommends that endpoint health checking features be enabled initially on a smaller cluster (3-10 nodes) where they can be used to detect potential packet loss due to firewall rules or hypervisor settings.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt recommends enabling the features initially on a smaller cluster, not disabling them immediately.
optionRationale.c: The recommendation is to enable them initially on a smaller cluster, not only after growing beyond 10 nodes.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt does not say endpoint health checking interferes with kube-proxy; it recommends enabling it initially on smaller clusters.

citations.title: Setup
citations.quote:
However it is recommended that those features be enabled
  initially on a smaller cluster (3-10 nodes) where it can be used to detect
  potential packet loss due to firewall rules or hypervisor settings.

questions.stem: How does Cilium distinguish an exclusive label pattern from an inclusive one in the identity-relevant label configuration?

options.text: Exclusive patterns are identified by the presence of the `!` character.
Exclusive patterns are identified by a leading `-` character.
Exclusive patterns are identified by the absence of any wildcard character.
Exclusive patterns are identified by being written in upper case.

questions.explanation: The excerpt explains that the listed label patterns are all exclusive label patterns, defining which label keys should be ignored, and that these are identified by the presence of the `!` character. Configurations without the `!` character are inclusive label patterns.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt names the ``!`` character, not a leading ``-``, as the marker.
optionRationale.c: Wildcards appear in both kinds of pattern, so their absence is not the distinguishing marker.
optionRationale.d: Case is not mentioned as a distinguishing feature anywhere in the excerpt.

citations.title: Limiting Identity-Relevant Labels
citations.quote:
The above label patterns are all *exclusive label patterns*, that is to say
they define which label keys should be ignored. These are identified by the
presence of the ``!`` character.

questions.stem: An engineer has applied an L7 CiliumNetworkPolicy that permits tiefighter to make only a POST /v1/request-landing call to deathstar. A colleague then runs `kubectl exec tiefighter -- curl -s -XPUT deathstar.default.svc.cluster.local/v1/exhaust-port`. What result should they expect?

options.text: The request is denied and the response reads `Access denied`.
The request succeeds and the response reads `Ship landed`.
The request causes deathstar to panic and explode.
The connection times out because tiefighter lacks the org=empire label.

questions.explanation: The excerpt shows that after the L7-aware policy is applied, the same PUT /v1/exhaust-port test produces `Access denied`, because the policy allows only POST /v1/request-landing and disallows all other calls, including PUT /v1/exhaust-port.

optionRationale.b: `Ship landed` is the response to the permitted POST /v1/request-landing call, not to the PUT to the maintenance API.
optionRationale.c: The panic and explosion output is what happened before the L7 policy was applied, in the illustrative example of unauthorised access.
optionRationale.d: The timeout applies to traffic from pods without the label org=empire, such as xwing; tiefighter is permitted by the identity-aware rule.

citations.title: Apply and Test HTTP-aware L7 Policy
citations.quote:
limiting *tiefighter* to making only a POST /v1/request-landing
API call, but disallowing all other calls (including PUT /v1/exhaust-port)

questions.stem: By default, which of the following does Cilium ignore when evaluating labels for identities?

options.text: All `k8s.io` labels
All `app.kubernetes.io` labels
All `reserved:` labels
All `io.cilium.k8s.policy.cluster` labels

questions.explanation: The excerpt lists the default exceptions to the rule that all labels are relevant for identities, and `!k8s\.io` is among them, described as ignoring all `k8s.io` labels.

optionRationale.b: ``app\.kubernetes\.io`` appears in the list of inclusive patterns automatically added when an inclusive pattern is configured, not in the default ignore list.
optionRationale.c: ``reserved:.*`` appears in the automatically added inclusive patterns, not in the default ignore list.
optionRationale.d: ``io\.cilium\.k8s\.policy\.cluster`` appears in the automatically added inclusive patterns, not in the default ignore list.

citations.title: Limiting Identity-Relevant Labels
citations.quote: ``!k8s\.io``                                        Ignore all ``k8s.io`` labels

questions.stem: During a migration run, the log shows that an identity's ID is already allocated to a different key in the CRD. What does the migration do for that key?

options.text: It aborts the migration and leaves the key unmigrated.
It reuses the old kvstore identity number for the key.
It allocates a new ID for the key in the CRD.
It deletes the conflicting CRD identity and keeps the kvstore one.

questions.explanation: The warning states that the ID is allocated to a different key in the CRD and that a new ID will be allocated for this key; the subsequent log line confirms a new ID was allocated for the key in the CRD.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt shows the migration continuing and allocating a new ID, not aborting.
optionRationale.b: The old identity is recorded (oldIdentity=11730) but a new ID (17281) is allocated, so the old number is not reused.
optionRationale.d: No deletion of the conflicting CRD identity is described; a new ID is simply allocated.

citations.title: Example migration
citations.quote: WARN[0003] ID is allocated to a different key in CRD. A new ID will be allocated for the this key

questions.stem: A user is configuring a `CiliumEnvoyConfig` resource manually. How is the proxy port for this resource determined, compared to an Ingress resource?

options.text: It is randomly assigned by the Cilium Ingress controller.
It is retrieved directly from the spec of the `CiliumEnvoyConfig` resource.
It is automatically selected from the range 10000-20000 by the kernel.
It is defined in the `cilium-config` ConfigMap under the `debug-verbose` key.

questions.explanation: The excerpt explicitly contrasts the two methods: for Ingress, the proxy port is randomly assigned by the Cilium Ingress controller, whereas for manually configured `CiliumEnvoyConfig` resources, the proxy port is retrieved directly from the spec.

optionRationale.a: This is the method used for Ingress resources, not manually configured `CiliumEnvoyConfig` resources.
optionRationale.c: While the `cilium-dbg status` output shows redirects active on ports 10000-20000, the excerpt does not state that the kernel selects the port for CEC resources; it states the port comes from the spec.
optionRationale.d: The `cilium-config` ConfigMap is used for flags like `debug` and `debug-verbose`, not for defining specific proxy ports for individual CEC resources.

citations.title: Connectivity Troubleshooting
citations.quote: For Ingress, the proxy port is randomly assigned by the Cilium Ingress controller. For manually configured ``CiliumEnvoyConfig`` resources, the proxy port is retrieved directly from the spec.

questions.stem: An engineer deploys Cilium with WireGuard encryption on nodes behind a restrictive firewall. Which port must the firewall allow for the WireGuard tunnel endpoint?

options.text: UDP 8472
TCP 4240
UDP 6081

questions.explanation: When WireGuard is in use, UDP port 51871 must be allowed.

optionRationale.b: UDP 8472 is the default VXLAN overlay port, not the WireGuard port.
optionRationale.c: TCP 4240 is used for cilium-health monitoring.
optionRationale.d: UDP 6081 is the Geneve overlay port.

citations.title: Firewall Rules
citations.quote: If you are using WireGuard, you must allow UDP port 51871.

questions.stem: Which mechanism does Cilium use to validate that an agent is able to receive key updates from etcd?

options.text: The operator constantly writes to a heartbeat key and all agents watch for updates to it.
Each agent acquires and releases a lock to test a write operation requiring quorum.
Each agent polls the etcd leader directly and compares the reported lease ID.
The Kubernetes liveness probe queries etcd on the agent's behalf.

questions.explanation: The excerpt describes the operator constantly writing to the heartbeat key cilium/.heartbeat, with all Cilium agents watching for updates, which validates the ability of an agent to receive key updates from etcd.

optionRationale.b: The lock acquisition and release tests a write operation requiring quorum; it is a separate check from validating receipt of key updates.
optionRationale.c: Polling the leader and comparing lease IDs is not described in the excerpt.
optionRationale.d: The liveness and readiness probes fail when Cilium reports failure; they are not described as querying etcd for the agent.

citations.title: Recovery behavior
citations.quote: The Cilium operator will constantly write to a heartbeat key (``cilium/.heartbeat``). All Cilium agents will watch for updates to this heartbeat key. This validates the ability for an agent to receive key updates from etcd.

questions.stem: A cluster uses Cilium in VXLAN overlay network mode, and Linux has not been configured otherwise for the VXLAN port. Which UDP port must be open among all nodes to enable the overlay?

options.text: UDP 8472
UDP 6081
TCP 4240

questions.explanation: In VXLAN overlay mode Cilium uses Linux's default VXLAN port 8472 over UDP unless Linux has been configured otherwise, so UDP 8472 must be open among all nodes.

optionRationale.b: UDP 6081 is the port used for Geneve overlay mode, not VXLAN.
optionRationale.c: UDP 51871 is the WireGuard encryption tunnel endpoint.
optionRationale.d: TCP 4240 is for cilium-health monitoring, not the VXLAN overlay.

citations.title: Firewall Rules
citations.quote:
If you are using VXLAN overlay network mode, Cilium uses Linux's default VXLAN
port 8472 over UDP, unless Linux has been configured otherwise.

questions.stem: A platform team runs Cilium on a cluster whose nodes are protected by a firewall that blocks all ICMP and TCP 4240 between nodes, but otherwise permits the traffic Cilium needs. The team asks what the consequence will be. What is the expected outcome?

options.text: Cilium will still operate fine, but it will not be able to provide health information.
Cilium agents will fail to start on the worker nodes until ICMP or TCP 4240 is opened.
Pod-to-pod traffic will be dropped because cilium-health is a prerequisite for the datapath.
Cilium will fall back to direct routing mode automatically to restore health monitoring.

optionRationale.d: This condition causes `XfrmOutStateSeqError`, not `XfrmInStateProtoError`.

questions.stem: An engineer has host policies in place on a set of nodes that must exchange VRRP advertisements with their peers. The host policy carries layer 3 and layer 4 rules, yet the VRRP traffic is being dropped with a DROP_CT_UNKNOWN_PROTO error. Which change allows this traffic through?

options.text: Add a layer 7 rule for the VRRP protocol to the host policy.
Install Cilium with the --enable-extended-ip-protocols flag set to true.
Add a layer 4 rule matching the transport-layer port that VRRP uses.
Install Cilium with --set devices='{interface}' pointing at the interface that carries the VRRP traffic.

questions.explanation: VRRP, IGMP and tunnel/encapsulation protocols have no transport-layer ports, so they cannot be matched by ordinary layer 4 port rules. To allow them, Cilium must be installed with the --enable-extended-ip-protocols flag set to true; without it such traffic is dropped by default with the DROP_CT_UNKNOWN_PROTO error. VRRP is listed among the supported extended protocols as protocol 112.

optionRationale.a: Host policies can carry layer 7 DNS rules but no other kinds of layer 7 rules, so a layer 7 rule for VRRP is not available.
optionRationale.c: VRRP is one of the protocols that have no transport-layer ports, so a port-based layer 4 rule cannot match it.
optionRationale.d: The devices flag only tells Cilium which network device the host firewall applies to, and Cilium auto-detects it if omitted; it does not enable extended IP protocols.

optionRationale.d: `XfrmOutPolBlock` is an XFRM error counter for packets Cilium dropped that would otherwise have left the node in plain-text; it is not the first thing to check when Pods fail to start.

Perform a new key rotation, properly, so that the SPI is incremented

optionRationale.b: The ipsec-key-rotation-duration flag controls how long before old keys are cleaned up after a rotation; it has nothing to do with a missing device warning.
optionRationale.c: A proper new key rotation is the fix given for XfrmInStateProtoError caused by a key update without incrementing the SPI, not for a missing interface warning.
optionRationale.d: Namespace co-location of the Secret and Cilium is the check for Pods that fail to start, not for a device warning in a running Pod's logs.

Set encryption.strictMode.ingress.enabled to true so that egress packets are encrypted before leaving the node.

optionRationale.b: The workaround is expressed as an egress policy restricting traffic to reserved:world, not an ingress policy dropping traffic from it.
optionRationale.c: Strict mode ingress concerns cluster-internal ingress traffic arriving other than through the WireGuard tunnel; it is not the workaround described for this egress issue.
optionRationale.d: Disabling encryption is not proposed; the aim is to prevent unencrypted traffic to arbitrary external targets while keeping encryption in place.

questions.stem: An engineer wants to stop pods in a Cilium cluster from sending unencrypted traffic to arbitrary targets outside the cluster, so that the window in which packets to not-yet-discovered remote endpoints leave unencrypted is closed. Which approach does Cilium describe as a workaround?

Define an ingress policy that drops all traffic from reserved:world identities, so that pods never receive replies from outside the cluster.
Enable encryption.strictMode.ingress.enabled so that all egress traffic leaving the node is encrypted.

optionRationale.b: The workaround is framed as an egress policy restricting where pods may send traffic, not an ingress policy on reserved:world.
optionRationale.c: Strict mode ingress concerns cluster-internal ingress traffic arriving other than through the WireGuard tunnel; it is not the egress workaround described.
optionRationale.d: allowRemoteNodeIdentities is a fallback that permits unencrypted traffic associated with a node identity; it does not prevent unencrypted egress.

questions.stem: In a Cilium TLS inspection deployment, which statement correctly describes the sensitivity of the CA private key and the CA certificate?

options.text: The CA private key must be kept safe because anyone with access to it can inspect TLS-encrypted traffic, whereas certificates are public information and not sensitive.
The CA certificate must be kept secret because it can be used to decrypt traffic, whereas the CA private key is public.
Both the CA private key and the CA certificate must be kept secret because either can be used to sign new certificates.
Neither the CA private key nor the CA certificate is sensitive because Cilium does not need either of them.

optionRationale.c: Only the private key is sensitive; certificates are public information.
optionRationale.d: The private key is extremely sensitive, and Cilium does need to be told which CAs to trust.

questions.stem: An endpoint in a Cilium cluster is permitted by policy to initiate traffic to destinations outside the cluster. A new node joins and runs a Cilium-managed pod, but the endpoint sends packets to that pod's IP address before Cilium has learned that the address belongs to a remote endpoint. What does Cilium do with those initial packets?

options.text: It drops them until the remote endpoint identity has propagated to every node.
It sends them unencrypted, then begins encrypting packets to that address once it learns the address is an endpoint on a remote node.
It encrypts them with the local node's key and re-encrypts them with the remote node's key after propagation.
It holds them in a queue until the remote node's encryption key is known, then forwards them encrypted.

questions.explanation: Transparent encryption uses the same mechanisms as policy enforcement to decide whether an outgoing packet's destination belongs to a Cilium-managed endpoint on a remote node. Until Cilium learns that the destination IP address belongs to a remote Cilium-managed endpoint or a newly joined remote Cilium host, it must assume the address is outside the cluster. During that time window it sends the initial packets unencrypted. Once the information has propagated and Cilium knows the address is an endpoint on a remote node, it starts encrypting packets using the encryption key of the remote node.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt describes a time window in which initial packets are sent unencrypted; it does not say that Cilium drops them while waiting for identity propagation.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt says Cilium starts encrypting with the remote node's key once it learns the address is a remote endpoint; it does not describe encrypting first with the local node's key and then re-encrypting.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says the initial packets are sent out unencrypted during the time window; it does not describe queuing them until the remote node's key is known.

optionRationale.c: While allowing traffic to reserved:world is a risk factor, the specific reason for the *initial* unencrypted packets to a *new* remote endpoint is the propagation delay of endpoint information, not the policy itself.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt does not state that the tunnel is disconnected; it states that Cilium assumes the destination is external until it knows otherwise.
