questions.stem: A network security team wants Cilium to inspect TLS-encrypted traffic destined for an external service. They generate an internal CA private key and CA certificate, then create a private key and certificate signing request for the destination, and use the CA private key to sign the certificate. What must also be done so that client workloads accept the inspected connection?

options.text: Install the internal CA certificate on each client workload so that they trust certificates signed by that CA.
Provide the internal CA private key to Cilium so that it can sign certificates on the fly.
Configure each client workload to trust the destination service's original certificate instead of the internal CA.
Disable TLS verification on the client workloads for the destination service.

questions.explanation: In the friendly interception model, the network security team creates an internal certificate authority and uses it to create alternative certificates for external destinations. For clients to accept these certificates, each client workload must trust the new certificate authority; otherwise the client's TLS library will reject the connection as invalid. The excerpt states: 'This model requires each client workload to also trust this new certificate, otherwise the client's TLS library will reject the connection as invalid.' Therefore, the CA certificate must be installed on the clients.

optionRationale.b: The CA private key is used only to create certificates, which can be done offline; it does not need to be provided to Cilium.
optionRationale.c: The client must trust the internal CA, not the destination's original certificate, because Cilium presents a certificate signed by the internal CA.
optionRationale.d: Disabling TLS verification is not mentioned and would undermine the authentication that TLS provides.

citations.title: A Brief Overview of the TLS Certificate Model

questions.stem: Encryption is enabled and the Cilium log files contain a `level=warning` message similar to `Device eth0 does not exist`. How should you resolve this?

options.text: Set the encryption interface explicitly with `--set encryption.ipsec.interface=ethX`.
Increase the delay before cleanup with the agent flag `ipsec-key-rotation-duration`.
Perform a new key rotation, properly, so that the SPI is incremented.
Verify that the IPsec `Secret` and Cilium are deployed in the same namespace together.

questions.explanation: The excerpt instructs you to check for `level=warning` and `level=error` messages in the Cilium log files, and states that if there is a warning message similar to `Device eth0 does not exist`, you should use `--set encryption.ipsec.interface=ethX` to set the encryption interface. The other options address different problems: key rotation timing, an SPI that was not incremented, and a namespace mismatch that prevents the Pods from starting at all.

optionRationale.b: ``ipsec-key-rotation-duration`` is used when you expect a key rotation to take longer, for example with Cluster Mesh; it does not address a missing device warning.
optionRationale.c: A proper new key rotation is the fix for ``XfrmInStateProtoError`` caused by a key update without incrementing the SPI, not for a device warning.
optionRationale.d: The namespace check applies when the ``cilium`` Pods fail to start after enabling encryption, which is a different symptom from a device warning in the logs.

citations.title: Troubleshooting

If there is a warning message similar to ``Device eth0 does not exist``,

     interface.

questions.stem: How does Cilium handle the start of additional pods labelled role=frontend once the first such pod has already been given an identity that is permitted to initiate connections to the identity of the role=backend pod?

options.text: It resolves the identity via a key-value store, with no action performed on any cluster node hosting role=backend pods.
It installs a new IP address filter on every node hosting a role=backend pod before the pod is allowed to start.
It assigns a fresh, unique identity to each new pod, which must then be separately allowed to reach the role=backend identity.
It delays the new pod until every cluster node has been updated with the security rules for that pod.

questions.explanation: Because Cilium bases security on a label-derived identity that can be shared between pods, starting further role=frontend pods only requires resolving that identity via a key-value store; nothing has to be done on the nodes hosting role=backend pods, and the start is delayed only until the identity is resolved.

optionRationale.b: Installing IP address filters on backend nodes is the traditional approach that Cilium replaces, not what Cilium does.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt states the identity can be shared between pods, so subsequent frontend pods reuse the existing identity rather than each needing a new one.
optionRationale.d: Updating security rules on all other cluster nodes is the costly step Cilium avoids; only identity resolution is required.

questions.stem: You have just enabled IPsec transparent encryption on a cluster and the `cilium` Pods fail to start. What should you check first?

options.text: Whether the IPsec `Secret` and Cilium are deployed in the same namespace together.
Whether the agent flag `ipsec-key-rotation-duration` is large enough for all agents to install the new key.
Whether the decryption interface list in `cilium-dbg encrypt status` includes every native device that may receive pod traffic.
Whether the `XfrmInNoStates` counter has increased while a new node key is being deployed.

questions.explanation: The excerpt gives a specific first check for this failure: if the `cilium` Pods fail to start after enabling encryption, double-check that the IPsec `Secret` and Cilium are deployed in the same namespace together. The other options are runtime diagnostics and tuning knobs that only become relevant once the agents are running: the key rotation duration governs how long the old key is kept, the decryption interface list is read from `cilium-dbg encrypt status`, and `XfrmInNoStates` counters rise during node reboots and key rotation.

optionRationale.b: The ``ipsec-key-rotation-duration`` flag is about delaying cleanup of the old key after a rotation, not about Pods failing to start.
optionRationale.c: The decryption interface list is a check performed with ``cilium-dbg encrypt status`` on a running Cilium Pod, so it cannot be the first thing to check when the Pods will not start.
optionRationale.d: ``XfrmInNoStates`` increases are expected while a new node key is being deployed after a node reboot, which presupposes running agents.

questions.stem: A three-node cluster has both IPv4 and IPv6 enabled and IPsec encryption is active. No key rotation is in progress. An engineer runs `cilium-dbg encrypt status` in a Cilium Pod and sees `Keys in use: 8`. What does this indicate?

options.text: The key count is as expected for this cluster configuration.
The key count is too high; it should be 4 because there are three nodes.
The key count is too low; it should be 12 because there are three nodes and two IP families.
The key count indicates that a key rotation is currently ongoing.

questions.explanation: The number of keys in use should be 2 per remote node per enabled IP family. In a three-node cluster with both IPv4 and IPv6 enabled and no key rotation, there should be 8 keys in use on each node, so 8 is correct.

optionRationale.b: The expected count is 2 per remote node per IP family, not 2 per node overall; with three nodes and two families the expected count is 8, not 4.
optionRationale.c: The expected count is 2 per remote node per IP family, giving 8 for three nodes and two families, not 12.
optionRationale.d: During a key rotation the count can double to 4 per remote node per IP family, which would give 16 here, not 8; 8 is the normal value.

questions.stem: A network security team wants Cilium to inspect TLS traffic destined for an external service. The CA private key is not needed by Cilium; it is used only to create certificates, which can be done offline.

optionRationale.b: The CA private key is used only to create certificates and does not need to be provided to Cilium at all.
optionRationale.c: Private keys for individual destination services are stored as Kubernetes secrets, but that is not what Cilium needs to validate the destination's certificate.
optionRationale.d: Clients need the CA certificate installed to trust certificates signed by that CA, but a client certificate is not what Cilium uses to validate the destination.

questions.stem: A Cilium cluster uses transparent encryption. An endpoint is permitted to initiate traffic to targets outside the cluster. A new pod is created on a remote node, and before information about that endpoint has propagated, the local endpoint sends packets to the new pod's IP address. What does Cilium do with those initial packets?

options.text: It sends them unencrypted, because it must assume the destination IP address is outside the cluster.
It drops them until the endpoint information has propagated to every node.
It encrypts them using the local node's key and re-encrypts them once the remote node is known.
It encrypts them using the encryption key of the remote node, which is fetched on demand for each packet.

questions.explanation: Transparent encryption decides whether to encrypt by using the same mechanisms as policy enforcement to determine whether the destination belongs to a Cilium-managed endpoint on a remote node. Until Cilium learns that an IP address belongs to a remote Cilium-managed endpoint or a newly joined remote Cilium host, it has to assume the destination is outside the cluster, so the initial packets go out unencrypted. Only once the endpoint information has propagated does Cilium begin encrypting using the remote node's key.

optionRationale.b: Nothing in the described behaviour involves dropping the packets; they are sent, but unencrypted, during the time window.
optionRationale.c: Cilium does not encrypt with the local key and then re-encrypt; it starts encrypting with the remote node's key once it knows the address is a remote endpoint.
optionRationale.d: The remote node's key is used only after Cilium has learned that the IP address is an endpoint on that remote node, not fetched per packet beforehand.

questions.stem: An engineer enables IPsec transparent encryption on a cluster and immediately finds that the `cilium` Pods will not start. Following the troubleshooting guidance for this section, what should be double-checked first?

questions.explanation: The excerpt's first troubleshooting step covers exactly this symptom: if the `cilium` Pods fail to start after enabling encryption, the thing to double-check is whether the IPsec `Secret` and Cilium are deployed in the same namespace together. The other checks in the excerpt address different symptoms — a missing device warning in the logs, the expected key count, and key rotation timing — and none of them is presented as the cause of Pods failing to start.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt pairs the IPsec ``Secret`` with Cilium's own namespace, not with the namespace of the workloads being encrypted.
optionRationale.c: Setting the encryption interface is the remedy for a ``Device eth0 does not exist`` warning in the logs, not for Pods that fail to start.
optionRationale.d: The key count is a health check performed with ``cilium-dbg encrypt status`` on a running Pod; it cannot be inspected while the Pods are not starting.

questions.stem: A host policy is in place and an operator needs VRRP traffic to be allowed on the nodes. What must be configured, and what happens to such traffic otherwise?

Add a layer 7 DNS rule for VRRP; without it, the traffic is rejected with a policy denial

optionRationale.c: hostFirewall.enabled is required to install host policies at all; it does not govern portless protocols.
optionRationale.d: VRRP has no transport-layer ports, which is precisely why the extended IP protocols flag is needed.

questions.stem: A Cilium cluster uses transparent encryption. A pod is permitted to initiate traffic to destinations outside the cluster. A new Cilium-managed endpoint is created on a remote node, but the local node has not yet learned that the endpoint's IP address belongs to that remote node. What happens to packets the pod sends to that IP address during this window?

options.text: Cilium sends the initial packets unencrypted because it must assume the destination IP is outside the cluster.
Cilium drops the packets until the endpoint information has propagated.
Cilium encrypts the packets using the local node's encryption key.
Cilium encrypts the packets using the remote node's encryption key as soon as the endpoint is created.

questions.explanation: Transparent encryption uses the same mechanisms as policy enforcement to decide whether a destination belongs to a Cilium-managed endpoint on a remote node. Until Cilium learns that a particular IP address belongs to a remote Cilium-managed endpoint or newly joined remote Cilium host, it has to assume the destination is outside the cluster and will send the initial packets unencrypted. Only once the information has propagated and Cilium knows the IP is an endpoint on a remote node does it start encrypting using the remote node's key.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt describes a time window during which packets are sent unencrypted, not dropped.
optionRationale.c: Encryption, once it begins, uses the encryption key of the remote node, not the local node.
optionRationale.d: Encryption with the remote node's key starts only after the endpoint information has propagated, not immediately on endpoint creation.

questions.stem: A cluster administrator wants to mitigate the risk of unencrypted egress traffic to not-yet-discovered remote endpoints by ensuring that traffic exiting a node to a specific set of IP addresses is always encrypted. Which configuration should they apply?

options.text: Set encryption.strictMode.egress.enabled to true and define the expected pod CIDR as encryption.strictMode.egress.cidr.
Enable encryption.strictMode.ingress.enabled to drop any cluster-internal ingress traffic that did not arrive via the WireGuard tunnel.
Configure a network policy that allows egress traffic to reserved:world identities to ensure all external traffic is routed through the tunnel.
Set encryption.strictMode.egress.allowRemoteNodeIdentities to false to block all traffic associated with node identities.

questions.explanation: The excerpt identifies setting encryption.strictMode.egress.enabled to true and the expected pod CIDR as encryption.strictMode.egress.cidr as a way to mitigate the issue by enforcing that traffic exiting a node to the set CIDR is always encrypted.

optionRationale.b: Strict mode ingress protects local endpoints from unencrypted ingress traffic, not egress traffic from the node to remote endpoints.
optionRationale.c: Allowing traffic to reserved:world is identified as a condition that makes the unencrypted leak possible, not a mitigation. The mitigation is to restrict this or use strict mode.
optionRationale.d: Setting allowRemoteNodeIdentities to false is not the primary mitigation described for the general pod CIDR; it is a specific setting related to node identities when not using direct routing mode.

citations.title: Egress traffic to not yet discovered remote endpoints may be unencrypted
citations.quote: Another way to mitigate this issue is to set ``encryption.strictMode.egress.enabled`` to ``true`` and the expected pod CIDR as ``encryption.strictMode.egress.cidr``. This encryption strict mode egress enforces that traffic exiting a node to the set CIDR is always encrypted.

questions.stem: A pod in a Cilium cluster with transparent encryption enabled is permitted by policy to initiate traffic to destinations outside the cluster. A new pod is created on a remote node, and the local node has not yet learned that the new pod's IP address belongs to a Cilium-managed endpoint. The local pod sends packets to that IP address during this window. What does Cilium do with those initial packets?

options.text: It sends them unencrypted, because it has to assume the destination IP address is outside of the cluster.
It drops them until the endpoint information has propagated, then retries them encrypted.
It encrypts them using the local node's key and re-encrypts them with the remote node's key once it learns the endpoint.
It encrypts them using the encryption key of the remote node, which it fetches on demand for each new destination.

questions.explanation: Transparent encryption uses the same mechanisms as policy enforcement to decide whether a destination belongs to a Cilium-managed endpoint on a remote node. Until Cilium learns that a particular IP address belongs to a remote Cilium-managed endpoint or newly joined remote Cilium host, it must assume the destination is outside the cluster, so the initial packets go out unencrypted. Only once the endpoint information has propagated does Cilium begin encrypting packets using the encryption key of the remote node.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt describes a time window in which packets are sent unencrypted; it does not describe dropping and later retrying them.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt says encryption uses the key of the remote node once the endpoint is known; it does not describe double encryption with the local key.
optionRationale.d: The key of the remote node is used once Cilium knows the IP address is an endpoint on a remote node, not fetched on demand before that.

citations.title: Egress traffic to not yet discovered remote endpoints may be unencrypted
citations.quote:
In such a case there is a time window during which Cilium will send out the
initial packets unencrypted, as it has to assume the destination IP address is
outside of the cluster.

questions.stem: A Cilium cluster uses transparent encryption. An endpoint is permitted to initiate traffic to targets outside the cluster. A new pod is created on a remote node, but the local node has not yet learned that the pod's IP address belongs to a Cilium-managed endpoint. During this time, the endpoint sends packets to that IP address. What does Cilium do with those initial packets?

options.text: It sends them unencrypted, because it must assume the destination IP address is outside the cluster.
It drops them until the endpoint information has propagated.
It encrypts them using the local node's encryption key.
It encrypts them using the encryption key of the remote node.

questions.explanation: Transparent encryption uses the same mechanisms as policy enforcement to decide whether a destination belongs to a Cilium-managed endpoint on a remote node. Until Cilium learns that a particular IP address belongs to a remote Cilium-managed endpoint or newly joined remote Cilium host, it has to assume the destination is outside the cluster, so the initial packets are sent unencrypted. Only once the information has propagated and Cilium knows the IP address is an endpoint on a remote node does it start encrypting packets using the encryption key of the remote node.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says the initial packets are sent out unencrypted, not dropped; dropping would be a policy action, not the described encryption behaviour.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt states that once the endpoint is known, encryption uses the encryption key of the remote node, not the local node's key.
optionRationale.d: Encryption with the remote node's key begins only after Cilium knows the IP address is an endpoint on a remote node; before that, packets are unencrypted.

citations.title: Egress traffic to not yet discovered remote endpoints may be unencrypted
citations.quote:
In such a case there is a time window during which Cilium will send out the
initial packets unencrypted, as it has to assume the destination IP address is
outside of the cluster.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes Path in Cilium?

options.text: Labels are used to identify the rule. Rules can be listed and deleted by labels. Policy rules which are imported via kubernetes automatically get the label ``io.cilium.k8s.policy.name=NAME`` assigned where ``NAME`` corresponds to the name specified in the `NetworkPolicy` or `CiliumNetworkPolicy` resource.
Description is a string which is not interpreted by Cilium. It can be used to describe the intent and scope of the rule in a human readable form.

Selects the endpoints or nodes which the policy rules apply to. The policy rules will be applied to all endpoints which match the labels specified in the selector. For additional details, see the EndpointSelector and NodeSelector sections.

Path is an extended POSIX regex matched against the path of a request. Currently it can contain characters disallowed from the conventional "path" part of a URL as defined by RFC 3986. Paths must begin with a ``/``. If omitted or empty, all paths are all allowed.

questions.explanation: Path is an extended POSIX regex matched against the path of a request. Currently it can contain characters disallowed from the conventional "path" part of a URL as defined by RFC 3986. Paths must begin with a ``/``. If omitted or empty, all paths are all allowed.

optionRationale.c: This describes endpointSelector / nodeSelector, not Path.
optionRationale.a: This describes labels, not Path.
optionRationale.b: This describes description, not Path.

citations.title: HTTP
citations.quote: Path is an extended POSIX regex matched against the path of a request. Currently it can contain characters disallowed from the conventional "path" part of a URL as defined by RFC 3986. Paths must begin with a ``/``. If omitted or empty, all paths are all allowed.

questions.stem: A policy contains two rules: one matches a narrow set of traffic and another matches a broader set that includes the narrow one. What does Cilium allow?

options.text: Only the traffic matching the narrow rule, since the broader rule is redundant.
All traffic matching the broader rule.
Only traffic matching the intersection of the two rules.
Nothing, because overlapping rules conflict and are dropped.

questions.explanation: Under the whitelist model, if one rule matches a broader set of traffic than another, all traffic matching the broader rule is allowed. Overlap does not create a conflict.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt says the broader rule's traffic is allowed, not that the narrow rule takes precedence.
optionRationale.c: The intersection is not the deciding factor here; the excerpt says traffic matching the broader rule is allowed.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt describes no conflict or drop for overlapping rules; it describes the union being allowed.

citations.title: Rule Basics
citations.quote:
If two rules exist, and one
would match a broader set of traffic, then all traffic matching the broader
rule will be allowed.

questions.stem: Which command opens a `bash` shell in one of the Cilium pods for the purpose of validating the WireGuard setup?

`kubectl -n kube-system exec -ti ds/cilium -- sh`
`kubectl -n default exec -ti ds/cilium -- bash`
`kubectl -n kube-system logs ds/cilium`

questions.explanation: The excerpt says to run a `bash` shell in one of the Cilium pods with `kubectl -n kube-system exec -ti ds/cilium -- bash`.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt specifies `bash`, not `sh`.
optionRationale.c: The namespace in the excerpt is `kube-system`, not `default`.
optionRationale.d: This retrieves logs rather than opening a shell.

Run a ``bash`` shell in one of the Cilium pods with
``kubectl -n kube-system exec -ti ds/cilium -- bash``

questions.stem: An engineer defines a Cilium Layer 7 HTTP policy rule that sets a Path regex but leaves the Method field empty. A client sends a POST request whose path matches the regex. What is the result?

options.text: The request is allowed, because an omitted or empty Method permits all methods.
The request is denied, because a Method must be specified explicitly for an HTTP rule to match.
The request is allowed only if it is a GET request, because GET is the default method.
The request is evaluated by matching the POST method against the Path regex.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that if Method is omitted or empty, all methods are allowed. The POST request is therefore permitted when its path matches the Path regex, and no separate Method value is required.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt does not require Method to be set; an omitted or empty Method allows all methods rather than causing a denial.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt says all methods are allowed when Method is omitted or empty, not that GET becomes the only permitted method.
optionRationale.d: Method is matched against the method of a request, while Path is matched against the path of a request; the two fields are not interchangeable.

citations.title: HTTP
citations.quote: Method is an extended POSIX regex matched against the method of a request, e.g. ``GET``, ``POST``, ``PUT``, ``PATCH``, ``DELETE``, ...  If omitted or empty, all methods are allowed.

questions.stem: You need to determine whether the derivative policy generated from a ToGroups rule is actually being enforced on a node, and when it was last updated. Which section of the derivative policy provides this?

options.text: status
metadata.labels
specs.Egress.ToCIDRSet
metadata.ownerReferences

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that status indicates whether or not the policy is enforced yet, and when the policy was last updated; the sample shows nodes with enforcing, lastUpdated and ok fields.

optionRationale.b: The labels identify the policy as a derivative and record its parent UUID, not its enforcement state.
optionRationale.c: ToCIDRSet holds the resolved destination IPs, not enforcement status or timestamps.
optionRationale.d: OwnerReferences links the derivative to its parent ToGroups policy.

citations.title: Validate that derived policy is in place
citations.quote:
- *status*: whether or not the policy is enforced yet, and when the policy was
  last updated.

questions.stem: An engineer is writing a CiliumNetworkPolicy for endpoints with label env=prod. They want to ensure that only source endpoints that also carry env=prod can reach those endpoints, but they do not want this rule alone to grant any access. Which field should they use to establish this base requirement?

options.text: fromRequires
fromEndpoints
toRequires
toEntities

questions.explanation: The fromRequires field establishes label requirements that serve as a foundation for any fromEndpoints relationship. It does not grant access by itself; additional rules matching fromEndpoints are needed to allow traffic. toRequires is for egress policies, fromEndpoints grants access, and toEntities is a different egress construct.

optionRationale.b: fromEndpoints is used to allow traffic from specific endpoints, not to set base requirements that do not grant access.
optionRationale.c: toRequires is the egress counterpart used with toEndpoints, not for ingress fromEndpoints.
optionRationale.d: toEntities is an egress rule that allows traffic to entities, not a base requirement field.

citations.title: Additional Label Requirements
citations.quote:
For this purpose, the ``fromRequires`` field can be used to establish label
requirements which serve as a foundation for any ``fromEndpoints``
relationship.

questions.stem: An engineer applies a manifest that creates a Deployment for each of three microservices and a Service named deathstar. The Service is intended to load-balance traffic to the deathstar pods across two replicas. Which label selector must the deathstar Service use for this to work?

options.text: org=empire, class=deathstar
org=empire, class=tiefighter
org=alliance, class=xwing
k8s-app=kube-dns

questions.explanation: The deathstar Deployment is identified with the labels (org=empire, class=deathstar), and the deathstar-service load-balances traffic to all pods carrying that label pair. The other label pairs belong to the tiefighter and xwing deployments, and k8s-app=kube-dns is the label shown on the DNS endpoints, not on the deathstar pods.

optionRationale.b: org=empire, class=tiefighter identifies the tiefighter landing-request client, not the deathstar webservice pods.
optionRationale.c: org=alliance, class=xwing identifies the alliance ship's client service, not the deathstar pods.
optionRationale.d: k8s-app=kube-dns appears on the coredns endpoints in the endpoint list, not on the deathstar pods.

questions.stem: An engineer is told that the Observer service exposes endpoints for Cilium agent events and Cilium datapath debug events. How do these endpoints differ from GetFlows?

options.text: GetAgentEvents and GetDebugEvents are similar to GetFlows except they do not implement filtering capabilities.
GetAgentEvents and GetDebugEvents are similar to GetFlows but add allow list and deny list filtering on top of it.
GetAgentEvents and GetDebugEvents are not part of the Observer service and are served by a separate principal service.
GetAgentEvents and GetDebugEvents return only a summary of GetNodes rather than event data.

questions.explanation: The excerpt says the Observer service also provides GetAgentEvents and GetDebugEvents to expose data about Cilium agent events and Cilium datapath debug events respectively, and that both are similar to GetFlows except they do not implement filtering capabilities.

optionRationale.b: This reverses the distinction: the excerpt says these endpoints do not implement filtering, whereas GetFlows does.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt explicitly places both endpoints within the Observer service.
optionRationale.d: Summarising GetNodes is the role of ServerStatus, not of these event endpoints.

citations.title: The Observer service
citations.quote:
Both are similar to ``GetFlows``
except they do not implement filtering capabilities.

questions.stem: A network engineer wants to configure Hubble metrics to include the Kubernetes namespace name for the source of the traffic. Which context option value should be used in the `sourceContext` configuration?

options.text: namespace
pod
identity
workload

questions.explanation: The table of option values lists `namespace` with the description 'Kubernetes namespace name'. The `pod` option includes both name and namespace, `identity` includes all security labels, and `workload` includes the workload name and namespace.

optionRationale.b: The `pod` option provides the pod name and namespace in the form of `namespace/pod`, which is more specific than just the namespace name.
optionRationale.c: The `identity` option provides all Cilium security identity labels, not just the namespace.
optionRationale.d: The `workload` option provides the workload name and namespace, not just the namespace.

citations.quote: ``namespace``         Kubernetes namespace name

questions.stem: A caller wants to read Cilium agent events from the Observer service and asks whether allow and deny list filters can be applied to that stream. What is the case?

options.text: GetAgentEvents is similar to GetFlows but does not implement filtering capabilities.
GetAgentEvents supports allow lists but not deny lists.
GetAgentEvents supports deny lists but not allow lists.
GetAgentEvents supports the same allow and deny list filters as GetFlows.

questions.explanation: Both GetAgentEvents and GetDebugEvents are similar to GetFlows except that they do not implement filtering capabilities.

optionRationale.b: No partial filtering support is described; neither allow nor deny filtering is implemented.
optionRationale.c: No partial filtering support is described; neither allow nor deny filtering is implemented.
optionRationale.d: Filtering is only described for GetFlows, not for GetAgentEvents.

citations.title: The Observer service
citations.quote:
Both are similar to ``GetFlows``
except they do not implement filtering capabilities.

questions.stem: An engineer configures a GetFlows request with an allow filter that matches a set of flows and a deny filter that matches a subset of those same flows. What will the resulting stream contain?

options.text: Only the flows that match the allow list and do not also match the deny list.
All flows that match either the allow list or the deny list.
Only the flows that match both the allow list and the deny list.
No flows, because allow and deny filters cannot be combined in a single GetFlows request.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that when both allow and deny filters are specified, the result contains all flows matched by the allow list that are not also simultaneously matched by the deny list. The deny filter therefore removes the overlapping subset from the allow-filtered set.

optionRationale.b: This treats the filters as a union, but the excerpt says the result is the allow-matched flows minus those also matched by the deny list.
optionRationale.c: This treats the filters as an intersection, but the excerpt says only one of multiple flow filters has to match and that the deny list removes flows from the allow list.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt explicitly describes combining allow and deny filters, so it is not true that they cannot be used together.

citations.title: The Observer service
citations.quote:
When both allow and
deny filters are specified, the result will contain all flows matched by the allow
list that are not also simultaneously matched by the deny list.

questions.stem: An engineer configures a Hubble metric with `flow:destinationContext=dns|ip`. For a particular flow the destination has no known DNS name. What label value is added to the metric for that flow?

options.text: The IP address of the destination, because the first non-empty value among the specified contexts is used.
An empty value, because the first listed context (`dns`) produced no value.
Both the DNS placeholder and the IP address, joined by the `|` symbol.
The value `reserved:world`, because an unresolved destination falls back to a reserved identity.

questions.explanation: When several contexts are separated by `|`, the first non-empty value is added as the label. The excerpt gives exactly this example: the DNS name is tried first, and if none is known the IP address is used instead.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt states the first non-empty value is used, so an empty first context does not stop the fallback.
optionRationale.c: The `|` symbol is the separator used in the configuration, not a joiner of values in the resulting label.
optionRationale.d: `reserved:world` is a reserved identity mentioned only in the context of the `reserved-identity` option, not a fallback for unresolved DNS.

citations.title: Context Options
citations.quote:
When multiple are specified, then the first non-empty value is added to the
metric as a label.

questions.stem: A caller issues a `GetFlows` request that supplies both an allow list and a deny list. A particular flow matches the allow list and also matches the deny list. What does the caller receive?

options.text: The flow is absent from the result, because the result contains only flows matched by the allow list that are not simultaneously matched by the deny list.
The flow is present, because a flow only needs to match one of the supplied filters to be included.
The flow is present, because the allow list always takes precedence over the deny list when both are supplied.
The flow is present twice, once for the allow list match and once for the deny list match.

questions.explanation: When both allow and deny filters are specified, the result contains all flows matched by the allow list that are not also simultaneously matched by the deny list. A flow that matches both lists is therefore excluded. The rule that only one of multiple flow filters has to match applies to filters of the same kind, and it does not override the interaction between an allow list and a deny list.

optionRationale.b: The 'only one has to match' rule describes multiple flow filters of the same kind; it does not mean a flow matching both an allow and a deny list survives.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt states the opposite: flows matched by the allow list are removed when they are also simultaneously matched by the deny list.
optionRationale.d: Nothing in the excerpt describes duplicate delivery; the deny list removes flows from the allow list result rather than adding to it.

citations.title: The Observer service
citations.quote: When both allow and deny filters are specified, the result will contain all flows matched by the allow list that are not also simultaneously matched by the deny list.

questions.stem: A Hubble instance has been running for a long time and its ring buffer has become full, while a ring reader in follow mode continues to read events as they are written. What happens to the events already stored in the buffer?

options.text: They are overridden by newer events, because events are continuously consumed and older ones are overridden once the ring buffer is full.
They are retained indefinitely and new events are dropped until the reader has drained the buffer.
They are written out to disk so that the in-memory buffer can be reused.
They are preserved because the ring buffer grows dynamically to accommodate new events.

questions.explanation: Hubble stores monitoring events in a user-space ring buffer that holds a configurable amount of events in memory. Events are continuously consumed, overriding older ones once the ring buffer is full, so the oldest stored events are lost as new ones arrive.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt describes older events being overridden, not new events being dropped while the reader catches up.
optionRationale.c: The buffer is described as storing events in memory; no spilling of events to disk is mentioned.
optionRationale.d: The buffer stores a configurable amount of events and overrides older ones when full; it is not described as growing dynamically.

citations.title: The Observer service
citations.quote: Events are continuously consumed, overriding older ones once the ring buffer is full.

questions.stem: An engineer finds that a hubble-relay pod is in `Pending` state. According to the troubleshooting guidance, what should the engineer do next?

options.text: Describe the pod with `kubectl describe -n kube-system pod/<pod-name>`.
View the pod logs with `kubectl -n kube-system logs <pod-name>`.
Delete the pod so that it is recreated.
Run `cilium status` again to confirm the error.

optionRationale.b: Viewing logs is recommended for pods that are not in Running state, not specifically for Pending pods.
optionRationale.c: Deleting the pod is not mentioned in the excerpt.
optionRationale.d: Running `cilium status` again is not the recommended action for a Pending pod; the excerpt directs the engineer to describe the pod.

citations.quote: If one or more pods are in ``Pending`` state, describe the pod(s) with:

questions.stem: A developer reads that the ring buffer's internal buffer length is a bit mask of ones plus one, with one slot reserved for the writer. From a user's perspective, what is the effective capacity of the ring buffer?

options.text: One less than a power of 2.
Exactly a power of 2.
One more than a power of 2.
An arbitrary value that is not constrained to a power of 2.

questions.explanation: The excerpt explains that the internal buffer size is always a power of 2 with 1 slot reserved for the writer, and that in effect, from a user perspective, the ring buffer capacity is one less than a power of 2.

optionRationale.b: A power of 2 describes the internal buffer size, not the user-visible capacity, which loses one slot to the writer.
optionRationale.c: The reserved slot is subtracted, not added, so the capacity is below a power of 2 rather than above it.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt states the internal buffer size is always a power of 2, so the capacity is constrained accordingly.

citations.title: The Observer service
citations.quote:
In effect, from a user perspective,
the ring buffer capacity is one less than a power of 2.

questions.stem: An engineer runs `cilium monitor` on a cluster where no L7 rules have been configured, and sees only L3/L4 packet events. She wants the tooling to surface DNS and HTTP flow details for Pods in the `default` namespace. What must she do?

options.text: Create a `CiliumNetworkPolicy` that specifies L7 rules, having first enabled L7 Proxy support.
Restart the Cilium agent with L7 proxy support disabled, since L7 visibility is a datapath-only feature.
Add an `endpointSelector` matching `k8s:io.kubernetes.pod.namespace: default` to a policy with only L3/L4 `toEndpoints` rules.
Run `hubble observe` with the `-t l7` filter, which by itself causes Cilium to start proxying matching traffic.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that L7 visibility requires enabling L7 Proxy support and that you enable visibility for L7 traffic by creating a `CiliumNetworkPolicy` that specifies L7 rules. Merely filtering output or writing L3/L4-only rules does not make L7 flows visible.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says the feature requires enabling L7 Proxy support, not disabling it, and describes L7 visibility as depending on redirection to the proxy.
optionRationale.c: A policy with only L3/L4 rules does not specify L7 rules, and the excerpt ties L7 visibility to policies that specify L7 rules.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt presents `hubble observe -f -t l7 -o compact` as a way to view L7 flow details once the policy is in place, not as the mechanism that enables proxying.

citations.title: Layer 7 Protocol Visibility
citations.quote:
To enable visibility for L7 traffic, create a ``CiliumNetworkPolicy`` that specifies
L7 rules.

questions.stem: An engineer wants to query flow events from pods running on every node of a cluster through a single Hubble endpoint, rather than contacting each node individually. Which Hubble component provides this multi-node capability?

options.text: Hubble Relay, which consumes the gRPC API of each Hubble instance to provide an API covering events from across the entire cluster
The Peer service, which itself aggregates and serves all flow events from every node
The Hubble server, which by default forwards events from all other nodes to the local client
The peer manager, which exposes the Observer service directly to external callers

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that Hubble Relay brings multi-node support, leveraging the Peer service to obtain information about Hubble instances and consuming their gRPC API to provide a richer API covering events from across the entire cluster. The Peer service supplies information about instances; it is Relay that consumes their APIs and serves the aggregated view.

optionRationale.b: The Peer service is used by Relay to obtain information about Hubble instances, not to aggregate and serve flow events itself.
optionRationale.c: The Hubble server instances make their API available per node; the excerpt does not describe the server forwarding other nodes' events.
optionRationale.d: The peer manager provides callers with the list of peers and handles reconnection; it is Relay that implements the Observer service for multi-node.

citations.title: Hubble Relay
citations.quote:
It leverages the Peer service to obtain information about Hubble instances and
consume their gRPC API in order to provide a more rich API that covers events
from across the entire cluster

questions.stem: A cluster administrator runs `cilium status` and sees that both `Cilium` and `Hubble Relay` report warnings or errors. What does this combination often indicate?

options.text: A misconfiguration in Hubble or the Hubble system failing to start.
The Cilium agent is not running.
Hubble Relay is disabled.
The cluster is healthy and Hubble is working correctly.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states: 'If warnings or errors are reported for both `Cilium` and `Hubble Relay`, it often hints at a misconfiguration in Hubble or the Hubble system failing to start.'

optionRationale.b: The excerpt notes that Cilium pods remain running and healthy even when Hubble fails, so Cilium not running is not implied.
optionRationale.c: If Hubble Relay were disabled, it would not report errors/warnings; the excerpt shows disabled components as 'disabled'.
optionRationale.d: Warnings or errors indicate a problem, not a healthy state.

citations.title: Hubble Relay
citations.quote:
If warnings or errors are reported for both ``Cilium`` and ``Hubble Relay``, it
often hints at a misconfiguration in Hubble or the Hubble system failing to start.

questions.stem: An engineer wants a list of namespaces that had network flows within the last one hour. Which Observer service RPC endpoint should be called?

options.text: GetNamespaces
GetNodes
ServerStatus
GetAgentEvents

questions.explanation: GetNamespaces returns a list of namespaces that had network flows within the last one hour.

optionRationale.b: GetNodes returns metrics and other information related to each Hubble instance.
optionRationale.c: ServerStatus returns a summary of the information in GetNodes.
optionRationale.d: GetAgentEvents exposes data about Cilium agent events, not namespaces with recent flows.

citations.title: The Observer service
citations.quote: ``GetNamespaces`` returns a list of namespaces that had network flows within the last one hour.

questions.stem: A developer is concerned about contention when many readers access the ring buffer on a hot code path. How has the ring buffer been designed in this respect?

options.text: It employs no locking mechanisms and uses atomic operations instead.
It uses a single global mutex around every read and write.
It uses a read-write lock that blocks writers while any reader is active.
It serialises all access through a dedicated lock-manager goroutine.

questions.explanation: As the ring buffer is a hot code path, it has been designed to not employ any locking mechanisms and uses atomic operations instead, which brings performance benefits but also complexity.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt explicitly states that no locking mechanisms are employed.

questions.stem: An engineer is writing a client that calls the Observer service's GetFlows endpoint and supplies both an allow list and a deny list of flow filters. What will the returned stream contain?

options.text: All flows matched by the allow list that are not also simultaneously matched by the deny list.

optionRationale.c: The excerpt describes the deny list as subtracting from the allow list result, not as the primary selection with the allow list as a fallback.

options.text: TLS is not enabled for the Hubble server, so the engineer should refer to the earlier configuration sections to enable TLS before continuing with the validation steps.

The peer is reachable only over the Unix socket, so the engineer should connect with `--server tls://${IP?}:4244` and the server name will then be displayed.

optionRationale.c: The excerpt does not link a missing `TLS.ServerName` to the `hubble-disable-tls` value; it only says to check that this option is set to `false` before beginning.

questions.stem: A team applies a `CiliumNetworkPolicy` containing L7 DNS and HTTP rules so that they can inspect application traffic. What side effect should they expect beyond gaining visibility?

questions.stem: A platform team runs Cilium 1.16 with Hubble metrics already enabled. They want the Hubble metrics API to be served over TLS, but they do not want Prometheus to have to present a client certificate. Which single Helm option should they add to their install or upgrade command?

optionRationale.b: This flag enables mTLS authentication on the metrics API, which would require clients to present certificates — more than the team asked for.
optionRationale.c: This flag only names the ConfigMap holding the CA certificate; it is used alongside the mTLS flags and does not on its own turn on TLS.

questions.stem: From the Hubble CLI pod you query the first peer with `hubble observe --server tls://${IP?}:4244 --tls-server-name ${SERVERNAME?} --tls-ca-cert-files /var/lib/hubble-relay/tls/hubble-server-ca.crt`, deliberately omitting the client certificate and key. What happens, and why?

options.text: The command fails with exit code 1 and a TLS error stating that a certificate is required, because the server expects clients to present a certificate.
The command succeeds, because supplying the CA certificate file is sufficient to authenticate the client to the server.
The command fails with `error reading server preface: EOF`, because the server only accepts plaintext connections on that port.
The command succeeds but returns only flows involving the host endpoint, since unauthenticated clients see a restricted view.

questions.explanation: The excerpt contrasts two attempts: one using the Hubble Relay client certificate, which confirms that the server accepts clients presenting the correct certificate, and one made without any client certificate, which fails with a TLS error reporting that a certificate is required and terminates with exit code 1. The CA file alone verifies the server; it does not authenticate the client.

optionRationale.b: The CA certificate file is used to verify the server's certificate; the excerpt shows the connection still failing when no client certificate is supplied.
optionRationale.c: The `EOF` error belongs to the separate attempt made without TLS at all, not to a TLS connection that lacks a client certificate.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt shows the command terminating with exit code 1 rather than returning a restricted set of flows.

questions.stem: An engineer is reasoning about how many events a Hubble ring buffer can hold, having read that the internal buffer length is a bit mask of ones + 1. Which statement describes the capacity from a user perspective?

options.text: The capacity is one less than a power of 2, because one slot is reserved for the writer.
The capacity is exactly a power of 2, with every slot available to readers.
The capacity is one more than a power of 2, because the writer slot is added on top of the mask.
The capacity is exactly the configured number of events, with no slot reserved for the writer.

questions.explanation: The internal buffer length is a bit mask of ones + 1, and the internal buffer size is always a power of 2 with 1 slot reserved for the writer. From a user perspective this means the ring buffer capacity is one less than a power of 2.

optionRationale.b: A power of 2 is the internal buffer size, but one slot is reserved for the writer, so the user-visible capacity is one less than that.
optionRationale.c: The reserved writer slot is taken out of the power-of-2 size rather than added to it, so the capacity is one less, not one more.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt explicitly reserves one slot for the writer, so the user-visible capacity is not the full configured figure.

citations.title: The Observer service
citations.quote: In effect, from a user perspective, the ring buffer capacity is one less than a power of 2.

`labelsContext` is only available for egress traffic, while `sourceContext` and `destinationContext` apply to both directions.

optionRationale.d: No such direction restriction is stated for `labelsContext`.

questions.stem: A Cilium operator configures a Hubble metric with `flow:destinationContext=dns|ip`. A flow targets a pod whose DNS name is not known to Hubble. What value is placed in the metric's `destination` label?

options.text: The IP address of the target, because the first non-empty value among the specified contexts is used.
An empty string, because the first context in the list (`dns`) produced no value.
Both the DNS name and the IP address, separated by a `|` symbol.
The literal string `dns|ip`, because multiple contexts cannot be combined for a single label.

questions.explanation: When multiple contexts are specified for source or destination, they are separated by `|` and the first non-empty value is added to the metric as a label. With `dns|ip`, Hubble first tries the DNS name; if none is known, it falls back to the IP address.

optionRationale.b: The fallback behaviour means an empty value is not used when a later context can supply a value.
optionRationale.c: Only one value is chosen; the `|` separates candidate contexts, not output values.
optionRationale.d: The `|` is a separator in the configuration, not a literal label value.

citations.title: Context Options

When multiple are specified, then the first non-empty value is added to the
metric as a label. For example, a metric configuration of
``flow:destinationContext=dns|ip`` will first try to use the DNS name of the
target for the label. If no DNS name is known for the target, it will fall back
and use the IP address of the target instead.

questions.stem: You are following the manual verification steps for monitoring generic IP options with Cilium. You want to inject a known Trace ID into packets sent from a client Pod to a server Pod, and you need a tool that can set IP options manually. Which approach does the tutorial take?

questions.stem: A cluster runs Cilium with Istio in ambient mode. options.text: All six checks return 200, because Istio's PERMISSIVE mode allows unsecured traffic between managed and unmanaged pods.
The three checks to httpbin.red return 200; the checks from red and blue to httpbin.blue return 200; the check from green to httpbin.blue returns 000 and the command terminates with exit code 28.
The three checks to httpbin.red return 200; all three checks to httpbin.blue return 000 and each command terminates with exit code 28.
The checks from red and blue to httpbin.blue return 403, while the check from green to httpbin.blue returns 000.

The expected output shows the green-to-blue check returning 000 with exit code 28, while the red and blue clients still reach httpbin.blue with 200 and all traffic to httpbin.red is unaffected. The 403 response appears only later, when an L7 policy is applied and a different URL path such as /deny is requested.

optionRationale.a: PERMISSIVE mode describes Istio's default handling of unsecured traffic between ambient-managed and unmanaged pods; it does not mean a Cilium L4 policy has no effect, and the checks do not all stay at 200.

questions.stem: How does the Cilium ingress controller expose its Envoy listener on the host when host network mode is enabled?

options.text: On all interfaces, using 0.0.0.0 for IPv4 and/or :: for IPv6.
Only on the loopback interface, using 127.0.0.1.
Only on the node's primary IP address, selected at startup.
On a ClusterIP address allocated by the LoadBalancer Service.

questions.explanation: In host network mode the listener is exposed on all interfaces, with 0.0.0.0 for IPv4 and/or :: for IPv6.

optionRationale.b: The listener is not restricted to loopback.
optionRationale.c: No selection of a single primary node IP is described; all interfaces are used.
optionRationale.d: Host network mode disables the LoadBalancer/NodePort Service mode, so no such Service address is used.

citations.title: Host network mode
citations.quote: The listener is exposed on all interfaces (``0.0.0.0`` for IPv4 and/or ``::`` for IPv6).

questions.stem: When multiple path types are configured on an Ingress object, in which order does Cilium configure Envoy with the matches?

Exact, ImplementationSpecific, Prefix, `/` Prefix
ImplementationSpecific, Exact, Prefix, `/` Prefix
Exact, Prefix, ImplementationSpecific, `/` Prefix

questions.explanation: The source lists the order as: 1. Exact, 2. ImplementationSpecific (that is, regular expression), 3. Prefix, 4. The `/` Prefix match has special handling and always goes last.

optionRationale.a: Incorrect. Prefix is listed third, not first.
optionRationale.c: Incorrect. Exact is listed first, not ImplementationSpecific.

questions.stem: A Cilium Gateway API HTTPRoute includes a RequestHeaderModifier filter with the configuration `remove: ["x-request-id"]` and a prefix match for `/remove-a-request-header`. A client sends a GET request to `http://$GATEWAY/remove-a-request-header`. The echo server returns a JSON body listing the request headers. Which header will be absent from that list?

options.text: X-Request-Id
X-Forwarded-For
X-Envoy-Internal
User-Agent

questions.explanation: The `remove` action in a RequestHeaderModifier filter removes the named headers from the incoming request. The excerpt shows that after applying `remove: ["x-request-id"]`, the `X-Request-Id` header no longer appears in the echo server's response, while `X-Forwarded-For`, `X-Envoy-Internal` and `User-Agent` remain present.

optionRationale.b: `X-Forwarded-For` is still present in the response after the removal filter is applied; it is not the header targeted by `remove`.
optionRationale.c: `X-Envoy-Internal` is still present in the response after the removal filter is applied; it is not the header targeted by `remove`.
optionRationale.d: `User-Agent` is still present in the response after the removal filter is applied; it is not the header targeted by `remove`.

Programmed

AttachedRoutes

questions.stem: An engineer creates an Ingress with two ImplementationSpecific paths, `/impl` and `/impl.*`, and expects requests to `/impl` to be handled by the first rule. What does Cilium actually do?

options.text: It sorts `/impl.*` ahead of `/impl` in the generated Envoy config, so the `/impl` match is never hit.
It sorts `/impl` ahead of `/impl.*` because the shorter string takes precedence within a path type.
It rejects the Ingress because two ImplementationSpecific paths may not overlap.
It treats both paths as Prefix matches, so `/impl` is matched exactly and `/impl.*` is ignored.

questions.explanation: Within each path type, paths are sorted in decreasing order of string length, so the longer `/impl.*` is placed ahead of `/impl`. Because `*` is in use, any request to `/impl` matches the regex `/impl.*` first, meaning the `/impl` match is never reached.

optionRationale.b: Sorting within a path type is in decreasing order of string length, so the longer regex path comes first, not the shorter one.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt describes no validation that rejects overlapping ImplementationSpecific paths; it only warns about the resulting behaviour.
optionRationale.d: ImplementationSpecific is defined by Cilium as Regex, not Prefix, and the excerpt does not say the second path is ignored.

citations.title: Ingress Path Types and Precedence
citations.quote: For example, if you have two ImplementationSpecific paths, ``/impl``, and ``/impl.*``, the second will be sorted ahead of the first in the generated config.

questions.stem: A developer notices that their backend service is receiving the IP address of the intermediate proxy instead of the original client IP. They are using a cloud load balancer that correctly injects the client IP into the X-Forwarded-For header. Which configuration change in the values file will force Envoy to treat the traffic as coming from the client IP encoded in that header?

options.text: Set useRemoteAddress to true in the gatewayAPI section.
Set useRemoteAddress to false in the gatewayAPI or ingressController sections.
Increase the number of trusted hops to 1 in the Envoy configuration.
Remove the X-Forwarded-For header from the incoming request before it reaches Envoy.

questions.explanation: The excerpt explicitly states that if you trust the source to inject an X-Forwarded-For header, you can force Envoy to treat the traffic as coming from the client IP encoded in the header by setting useRemoteAddress to false in gatewayAPI or ingressController sections of values files.

optionRationale.a: Setting useRemoteAddress to true would likely maintain the default behaviour of using the remote address, whereas the excerpt specifies setting it to false to use the header value.
optionRationale.c: While increasing trusted hops affects which value in the list is used, the specific mechanism described for trusting the injected header in the context of gatewayAPI/ingressController values is setting useRemoteAddress to false.
optionRationale.d: Removing the header would prevent Envoy from seeing the client IP, which is the opposite of the desired outcome.

citations.title: Source IP Visibility
citations.quote: If you trust the source of the traffic to inject an ``X-Forwarded-For`` header (such as when using a cloud load balancer), you can force Envoy to treat the traffic as coming from the client IP encoded in the ``X-Forwarded-For`` header by setting ``useRemoteAddress`` to ``false`` in ``gatewayAPI`` or ``ingressController`` sections of values files.

questions.stem: You have a local Kubernetes cluster running Cilium and Istio, and you want to follow the demo setup for Istio sidecar mode. Which combination of Helm values must Cilium have been installed with?

options.text: `socketLB.hostNamespaceOnly` and `cni.exclusive=false`
`socketLB.enabled=false` and `cni.exclusive=true`
`socketLB.hostNamespaceOnly` and `cni.exclusive=true`
`socketLB.enabled=true` and `cni.exclusive=false`

questions.explanation: The prerequisites state that Cilium must already be installed with the `socketLB.hostNamespaceOnly` and `cni.exclusive=false` Helm values. Both values must match exactly; changing either one departs from the stated prerequisite.

optionRationale.b: This inverts both values: it disables socket LB and makes the CNI exclusive, neither of which appears in the prerequisites.
optionRationale.c: The socket LB value is right, but ``cni.exclusive`` is set to true rather than the required false.
optionRationale.d: The ``cni.exclusive=false`` part is right, but ``socketLB.enabled=true`` is not the value named in the prerequisites.

citations.title: Prerequisites
citations.quote: Cilium is already installed with the ``socketLB.hostNamespaceOnly`` and ``cni.exclusive=false`` Helm values.

questions.stem: An engineer is configuring a Cilium gateway to handle traffic from a cloud load balancer that injects the client IP into the X-Forwarded-For header. By default, how does Cilium's Envoy instance determine the trusted client address for policy enforcement?

options.text: It uses the address the connection is opened from, as the default number of trusted hops is set to 0.
It uses the first value in the X-Forwarded-For list, counting from the left.
It uses the last value in the X-Forwarded-For list, counting from the right.
It ignores the X-Forwarded-For header entirely and relies solely on the TCP source IP without any header processing.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that by default, Cilium sets the number of trusted hops to 0, indicating that Envoy should use the address the connection is opened from, rather than a value inside the X-Forwarded-For list.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt specifies that increasing the count uses the nth value counting from the right, not the first from the left, and the default is 0 hops (connection address).
optionRationale.c: While the logic for non-zero hops counts from the right, the default is 0 hops, which means it uses the connection address, not a value from the list.
optionRationale.d: Envoy does process the header to set X-Envoy-External-Address, but for determining the trusted client address with 0 trusted hops, it uses the connection address, not ignoring the header mechanism entirely in the context of the configuration logic described.

citations.title: Source IP Visibility
citations.quote: That is, by default Cilium sets the number of trusted hops to ``0``, indicating that Envoy should use the address the connection is opened from, rather than a value inside the ``X-Forwarded-For`` list.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes the relationship between the Cilium operator and SPIRE entries for workloads?

options.text: The Cilium operator registers Identities with the SPIRE server on behalf of the workloads (Kubernetes Pods).
The Cilium agent registers Identities with the SPIRE server on behalf of the workloads.
The SPIRE server registers Identities with the Cilium operator on behalf of the workloads.
Workloads register their own Identities directly with the SPIRE server.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that the Cilium operator should have registered Identities with the SPIRE server on behalf of the workloads (Kubernetes Pods).

optionRationale.b: The Cilium agent has a delegate Identity but does not register workload identities; that is done by the operator.
optionRationale.c: The direction is reversed: the operator registers with the SPIRE server, not the other way around.
optionRationale.d: Workloads do not register themselves; the operator does it on their behalf.

citations.title: Verify SPIFFE Identities
citations.quote: The Cilium operator should have registered Identities with the SPIRE server on behalf of the workloads (Kubernetes Pods).

questions.stem: An engineer is exposing Cilium's Envoy DaemonSet through a Loadbalancer Service in a cluster that uses kube-proxy. They need the backend pod to see the client's source IP. Which externalTrafficPolicy setting is the only way to ensure source IP visibility in this cluster?

options.text: Local
Cluster
External
None; source IP visibility is not affected by externalTrafficPolicy.

questions.explanation: With externalTrafficPolicy: Local, nodes route traffic only to Pods running on the local node without masquerading the source IP. In clusters that use kube-proxy, this is the only way to ensure source IP visibility.

optionRationale.b: With Cluster, the node may masquerade the source IP, so the backend pod may not see it.
optionRationale.c: External is not one of the two relevant settings described for externalTrafficPolicy.
optionRationale.d: The field is described as particularly relevant to Client IP visibility, so this is incorrect.

citations.title: ``externalTrafficPolicy`` for Loadbalancer or NodePort Services
citations.quote:
``Local``: Nodes will only route traffic to Pods running on the local node, 
  *without masquerading the source IP*. Because of this, in clusters that use
  ``kube-proxy``, this is the only way to ensure source IP visibility.

questions.stem: In a deployment where Istio ambient mode uses mTLS together with Istio L7 HTTP policy controls, how does Cilium NetworkPolicy apply to traffic between the Istio-managed, mTLS-secured workloads?

options.text: Cilium enforces L7 policy on the decrypted HTTP requests inside the tunnel.
Cilium NetworkPolicy applies to the encrypted and tunneled L4 traffic, but Cilium has no visibility into the actual source and destination or any L7 information.
Cilium NetworkPolicy does not apply at all because the traffic is encrypted.
Cilium enforces policy only on traffic entering from non-Istio-managed workloads.

questions.explanation: When Istio mTLS is used in ambient mode with Istio L7 policy controls, traffic between ambient workloads is encrypted and tunnelled by Istio over port 15008. Cilium NetworkPolicy still applies to that encrypted and tunnelled L4 traffic, but Cilium cannot see the real source and destination or any L7 details.

optionRationale.a: Cilium has no visibility into L7 information for this tunnelled and encrypted traffic.
optionRationale.c: Cilium NetworkPolicy still applies to the encrypted and tunnelled L4 traffic; it is not bypassed entirely.
optionRationale.d: Traffic from non-Istio-managed workloads is a separate case; the question asks about traffic between Istio-managed workloads.

citations.title: Istio configuration
citations.quote:
Cilium NetworkPolicy will still apply to the encrypted and tunneled L4 traffic entering and leaving the Istio-managed pods,

questions.stem: When you inspect the SPIRE entry for the echo Pod, the `Parent ID` field shows `spiffe://spiffe.cilium/cilium-operator` rather than the SPIRE agent. Why?

options.text: The echo Pod is running in the kube-system namespace with the cilium-operator service account.
The Cilium operator creates SPIRE entries for Cilium Identities as they are created.
The SPIRE agent delegates all workload registrations to the Cilium agent, which forwards them to the operator.
The entry was registered manually and the Parent ID must be corrected to the SPIRE agent.

questions.explanation: The excerpt explains that the cilium-operator appears in the `Parent ID` because the Cilium operator creates SPIRE entries for Cilium Identities as they are created. This is also stated earlier: the operator registers Identities with the SPIRE server on behalf of the workloads.

optionRationale.a: The kube-system namespace and cilium service account selectors belong to the cilium-agent entry, and kube-system with cilium-operator to the operator entry; neither describes the echo Pod.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt describes no such forwarding chain; it says the operator registers Identities on behalf of the workloads.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt presents the operator as parent as expected behaviour, not as an error to be corrected.

citations.title: Verify SPIFFE Identities
citations.quote: That is because the Cilium operator creates SPIRE entries for Cilium Identities as they are created.

Disable Cilium's L7 policy enforcement.
Switch Istio from PERMISSIVE to STRICT mode.
Remove the Cilium L4 network policy.

optionRationale.b: Disabling Cilium's L7 policy would prevent Cilium from managing L7 policy, which is the goal.

optionRationale.d: Removing the L4 policy does not address the mTLS interference with L7 policy.

The Cilium agent created the SPIRE entry on behalf of the workload.

questions.stem: A cluster uses Istio ambient mode with Istio mTLS and Istio L7 HTTP policy controls. Traffic between two ambient workloads is encrypted and tunneled by Istio over port 15008. What can Cilium NetworkPolicy do with that traffic?

options.text: It still applies to the encrypted and tunneled L4 traffic entering and leaving the Istio-managed pods, but Cilium has no visibility into the actual source and destination or any L7 information.
It is bypassed entirely, because Istio takes over all policy enforcement for ambient workloads.
It can inspect the L7 HTTP details inside the tunnel and enforce HTTP-level rules on them.
It applies only after Istio decrypts the traffic and hands it back to Cilium for L7 inspection.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that in this scenario Cilium NetworkPolicy will still apply to the encrypted and tunneled L4 traffic entering and leaving the Istio-managed pods, but Cilium will have no visibility into the actual source and destination of that traffic, or any L7 information.

optionRationale.b: Cilium policy is not bypassed; it still applies to the tunneled L4 traffic.
optionRationale.c: Cilium has no visibility into any L7 information for this tunneled and encrypted traffic.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says nothing about Istio handing decrypted traffic back to Cilium; it says Cilium has no visibility into source, destination or L7.

questions.stem: A platform team runs a shared cluster. They want application developers in one team to be able to publish HTTP routes for their own services, but they must not be able to change the shared Gateway configuration or touch Route objects in other teams' namespaces. Which characteristic of the Gateway API supports this arrangement?

options.text: The Gateway API is designed with role-based personas in mind, and deconstructing the Ingress API into several objects lets each persona gain only the access and privileges their responsibilities require.
The Gateway API removes the need for annotations, which makes resources portable between implementations and therefore lets any developer edit any object.
The Gateway API provides extension points that promote features to API conformance, which automatically scopes Route objects to a single namespace.
The Gateway API centralises HTTP routing, TLS termination, traffic splitting and header modification in a single object that only infrastructure providers may create.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that the Gateway API is designed with role-based personas in mind and that, by deconstructing the Ingress API into several Gateway API objects, personas gain the specific access and privileges that their responsibilities require. It gives exactly this example: developers in a team could be given permission to create Route objects in a specified namespace without permission to modify the Gateway configuration or edit Route objects in other namespaces.

optionRationale.b: Annotation-free portability is mentioned in the excerpt, but it is a separate benefit and does not grant developers access to arbitrary objects.
optionRationale.c: Extension points and promotion of features to API conformance are described, but the excerpt does not say they scope Route objects to a namespace.
optionRationale.d: The centralised policy mechanism is described, but the excerpt does not say it is a single object restricted to infrastructure providers.

citations.title: Benefits of the Gateway API
citations.quote: By deconstructing the Ingress API into several Gateway API objects, personas gain the specific access and privileges that their responsibilities require.

`set`
`add`
`delete`

optionRationale.b: `set` is used to edit an existing header's value, not to delete it.
optionRationale.c: `add` is not mentioned as a removal keyword in the excerpt.
optionRationale.d: `delete` is not the keyword used; the excerpt uses `remove`.

questions.stem: An engineer runs `kubectl get gateway -A` and receives an error that the resource type `Gateway` is not found. What should the engineer check?

options.text: Whether the Gateway API CRDs are installed.
Whether the Gateway class is set to `cilium`.
Whether a LoadBalancer service is assigned to the Gateway.
Whether the Gateway is programmed.

questions.explanation: If the Gateway API resource type (such as `Gateway` or `HTTPRoute`) is not found, the engineer should make sure that the Gateway API CRDs are installed. The other checks apply only once the resource type exists and can be listed.

optionRationale.b: The class check is relevant only after the Gateway resource is found.
optionRationale.c: The LoadBalancer check is relevant only after the Gateway resource is found.
optionRationale.d: The programmed status is relevant only after the Gateway resource is found.

questions.stem: An engineer lists all SPIRE entries with `-selector cilium:mutual-auth` and then runs `kubectl get ciliumidentities`. How should the engineer confirm that the two sets match?

options.text: The identity ID listed under NAME in the ciliumidentities output should match the digits at the end of each SPIFFE ID.
The Entry ID of each SPIRE entry should match the identity ID under NAME.
The Parent ID of each SPIRE entry should match the identity ID under NAME.
The Selector of each SPIRE entry should match the identity ID under NAME.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that the identity ID listed under NAME should match with the digits at the end of the SPIFFE ID.

optionRationale.b: The Entry ID is a UUID for the SPIRE entry, not the Cilium Identity ID.
optionRationale.c: The Parent ID identifies the parent agent or operator, not the Cilium Identity ID.
optionRationale.d: The Selector is a label such as `cilium:mutual-auth`, not the Cilium Identity ID.

citations.title: Verify SPIFFE Identities
citations.quote: The identify ID listed under ``NAME`` should match with the digits at the end of the SPIFFE ID executed in the previous command.
